a153ff01be906453: Microsoft has slipped some bad news into this week's Ignite AI puffery: the To Do apps are retiring on June 30, 2027, ending a journey that began with its acquisition of Wunderlist more than a decade ago.

The confirmation came in an announcement about unified tasks and plans for Copilot and Microsoft 365. Until now, there was To Do or Planner (in basic or premium guise). The idea is "a single system for tracking your work as an individual, as a team, and as an organization." To Do contributes features to that future, but its apps don't get to join it.

The problem is that Planner doesn't do everything To Do does. Microsoft would like users to migrate to Planner but, by the company's own admission, there are plenty of gaps. No native Windows or Mac desktop apps are planned to replace To Do; file attachments aren't supported on tasks in the Planner private plan, and there's no equivalent to To Do list groups in Planner. "Equivalent To Do printing and email-list capabilities are not currently planned for the replacement experience," and so on.

Existing To Do tasks and lists won't migrate to Planner either. They'll remain accessible through Planner until June 30, 2027, but that access ends with the apps. Microsoft says the date does not itself trigger deletion of the underlying data.

Personal Microsoft account holders are left in an even worse state: Planner isn't available to them, including Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscribers. Microsoft's advice is to choose another task-management app and prepare to export their data. Export instructions are still to come, and exporting won't necessarily produce something another app can import.
Very much a case of "don't let the door hit you on the way out."

Unifying tasks and plans is a good idea – the current situation does create confusion, as Microsoft acknowledged. However, taking an axe to To Do, which was developed to be a successor to Wunderlist (acquired in 2015 for a figure between $100 million and $200 million, an early action under Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella), seems extreme.

Microsoft calls the replacement "a unified platform for people and agents across Microsoft 365" and stated: "This unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier."

Some users responding to the announcement were unimpressed, with one declaring "What a mess," and another asking if To Do might be spun off into an open source project: "Not everything needs to be put into an AI/Copilot agent."
Indeed, it doesn't. But a useful service that doesn't ram Copilot and AI integration down customers' throats at every opportunity? That would never do.
The message for To Do users appears to be: Get with the Plan(ner) or just get out. ®
c66fd6e4f18db99e: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.
While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”

Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.
Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”
“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”
866c236a92cc7cbe: An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the company's delay in notifying them.
Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days.
Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable."

News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday.
Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6.
Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days.
The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them.
The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types:
Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames
Business Identifier Codes (BICs)
International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs)
Sort codes
Payment references
Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers
Payee addresses

Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds.
St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach.
The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data."
He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.
Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations.

"We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses."
Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services.
Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said.
Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations.
Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time.
"What's most important is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he said.
Separately, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Bank of England opened a joint consultation on cyber resilience guidance on Thursday.

The FCA said October brought its second-highest monthly tally of reported cyber incidents in five years, and the highest in 18 months. The proposed guidance clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements rather than introducing new rules. ®

0eb8111972cbbde0: PETALING JAYA: Big Caring Group Bhd’s debut on Bursa Malaysia’s Main Market ended with little fanfare for Malaysia’s largest retail pharmacy chain operator.
Shortly after the opening bell, the stock fell to its intraday low of 98 sen, 9.3% or 10 sen below its initial public offering (IPO) price of RM1.08 per share.
It then rebounded to its intraday high of RM1.19 – 10% or 11 sen above its IPO price – before giving back these gains to close one sen or 0.9% higher at RM1.09, valuing the group at RM8.04 billion.
Big Caring’s listing nevertheless garnered investors’ attention as it was the most traded stock on Bursa Malaysia with 572.85 million shares changing hands, valued at over half a billion ringgit.
The focus on Big Caring is understandable as applications from retail investors came in at more than four times the number of shares available for subscription.

The company previously said the IPO will involve up to 1.9 billion shares, representing 25.5% of its enlarged share capital. Of this, 590.5 million new shares will be issued while 1.3 billion existing shares will be offered for sale.

The IPO comprised 267.6 million shares offered to retail investors and an institutional tranche of up to 1.6 billion shares, of which 19 cornerstone investors subscribed for 41.2% of the institutional offering.
Big Caring is helmed by group managing director and CEO Lee Meng Chuan and his wife Lim Sin Yin, who opened their first outlet in Damansara Uptown, Selangor, in 2006.
The group has grown rapidly since and has 668 outlets controlling nearly a quarter of the market share as at end-September.

Its expansion was fuelled by a combination of organic growth and strategic acquisitions, including the merger with RedCap Pharmacy in 2018 and My Pharmacy in 2019. It then acquired Caring Pharmacy from 7-Eleven Malaysia Holdings Bhd in 2023.
Apart from the Big Pharmacy and Caring Pharmacy chains, brands under its wing include Georgetown Pharmacy, Wellings, Ting Pharmacy, and iCare Pharmacy.

Funds raised from the public issue of new shares totalling RM637.8 million are mainly to reduce debt incurred from the high-profile acquisitions and set up a RM30 million distribution centre in Klang.

As at end-August, Big Caring’s bank borrowings totalled RM1.7 billion, with the bulk of this debt being a RM831.3 million term loan used primarily for its RM888.3 million acquisition of Caring Pharmacy Group Sdn Bhd.
It also forked out RM249.4 million for an 89.3% stake in pharmaceutical distributor Medispec (M) Sdn Bhd, and RM32.8 million for a controlling stake in physiotherapy chain Your Physio.

An offer for sale of existing shares raised RM1.33 billion which went to a group of shareholders including Uptown Paradise Sdn Bhd led by Lee and private equity firm Creador, which will hold a 19% stake following the listing.

e1a149bd991cbc8c: Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers.

The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise.

"We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," said Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident."

TfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did.
TfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected.

Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over.

Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too.

TfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems.

Existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action. There's no word yet on when it'll be back.
"We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma said.

TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised.

Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement action against TfL, having deemed its response proportionate. There's nothing at present to suggest the two incidents are related.
Londoners can at least rest assured that their Oyster photocards still work. Whether the information they handed over to obtain them is in someone else's hands is another matter. ®

While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.
We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.
Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)
I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”

a2c0df1404e712c0: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note.

Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see.

During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not.

"Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door."

Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee.

Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries.

The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically.
The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records.

"At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said.

After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in.

The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information.

"The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®

6b61b4736011fe25: Uncensored large language models (ULLMs) capable of producing harmful content are readily available at popular model-hosting websites, calling into question AI industry commitments to safety.

Researchers affiliated with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in the US and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore have analysed 22,096 ULLMs collected from five major LLM hosting platforms.

As described in their paper, "Characterizing the Ecosystem of Open-Source Uncensored Large Language Models: Supply Chain, Governance, and Risks," authors Zilong Lin, Zichuan Li, Xiaojing Liao, and XiaoFeng Wang found that uncensored LLMs are easy to obtain from hosting platforms like US-based Hugging Face, Kaggle, and John Snow Labs, and China-based OpenCSG and ModelScope.

What's more, these unrestrained models have been deployed through applications, GitHub projects, and model routing platforms like Open Router, and users of those apps or services may not be aware of the nature of the underlying LLM.

"Uncensored LLMs generally refer to LLMs whose content filtering or refusal safeguards are absent, removed, or weakened, allowing them to respond to requests that aligned models may refuse," the paper explains.

Zilong Lin, lead author and assistant professor of computer science at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, told The Register that open source LLM hosting platforms like Hugging Face play a similar role to code hosting services like GitHub, GitLab, and Codeberg in the open source community by enabling sharing, modification, and redistribution of code artifacts.

"However, unlike traditional software, whose behavior can often be examined through source code analysis, the safety alignment of LLMs is difficult to assess directly from their model files," Lin explained. "Evaluating whether an LLM has adequate safety safeguards typically requires deploying the model and testing its responses to potentially harmful prompts, which involves substantial computational and financial costs."

Lin said this makes the identification and assessment of LLM safety particularly challenging, particularly given the large number of models available. That's why he and his colleagues chose to study the space through publicly available model metadata.

Even popular commercial LLMs that are purportedly "aligned" – to some standard not everyone accepts – may respond to prompts with content deemed harmful. The US Government Accountability Office just released a report that found Claude, Grok, ChatGPT, and Gemini can be coaxed to provide information that would help with the planning of a terror attack.

To highlight the consequences of AI advice, the GAO points to news reports indicating that generative AI helped enable the creation of an explosive device in a January 2025 attack on a Las Vegas hotel and the planning of a February 2026 mass shooting in British Columbia, Canada.

The issue with open weight LLMs is that anyone with modest technical skills (or just cluelessly assisted by a compliant LLM) can apply techniques like toxic training/fine-tuning (TTFT) or de-aligned training/fine-tuning (DTFT) to datasets that haven't been safe, in order to produce models with reduced or removed refusal behavior. Examples include toxicqa-Llama2-13B and WizardLM-7B-Uncensored. A more recent technique called refusal-direction ablation (or abliteration, e.g., Daredevil-8B-abliterated) dilutes refusal training to make the model less likely to refuse requests.

Uncensored (or simply less restrictive) models have legitimate uses, sometimes ironically because commercial models are insufficiently permissive and refuse legitimate security analysis. Hugging Face, for example, had to resort to using Z.ai's less rule-encumbered GLM-5.2 to analyze the hacking of its infrastructure by OpenAI's irresponsibly unsupervised AI agents.
But ULLMs can just as easily be misused to provide guidance about illegal activity, assist with malware development, or emit content that's harmful, malicious, or manipulative in some way.
"We identified more than 11,000 ULLMs appearing across multiple platforms, with Hugging Face serving as the dominant upstream source," Lin said in a blog post.

"This movement exposes an important governance gap: models can travel more easily than the information needed to assess their risks. Only about 13 percent of the ULLMs we identified carried moderation warnings, and security threat indicators were not consistently preserved across platforms.
"This creates a supply chain problem: a model can be copied across platforms while the information needed to understand its risks is lost along the way."

The ULLMs were evaluated for text output and not images. The issues raised by text-to-image LLMs, such as the ability to generate illegal images (e.g. CSAM), were beyond the scope of this particular study.

"The uncensored LLMs we evaluated were generally more likely to comply with harmful requests and generate harmful content than non-uncensored models," Lin said. "Our evaluation covered 11 categories of harmful requests, including child abuse, illegal activities, and fraud.

"However, the ability of an individual model to generate harmful content varies depending on several factors, including its training data, development methods, and the extent to which its refusal direction has been ablated."

A small portion of these ULLMs (27 of them, which have been downloaded 136,000 times) exhibited threat indicators from security scans. Many of these, authors say, had signatures associated with malware, exhibited suspicious binary patterns, or contained unsafe deserialization mechanisms that could allow arbitrary code execution.
From trickle to flood

The number of ULLMs has been rising rapidly, according to the paper, from about 100 per month in May 2023 to more than 1,000 per month presently. And some of these models have been downloaded millions of times. The uncensored model dolphin-2.9.1-yi-1.5-34b has more than 53 million downloads, and more than 4.8 million just last month.

The authors note that many ULLMs violate the licensing terms of the models on which they've been based, not that source code licensing has had any meaningful impact on the behavior of the AI industry.

Asked whether the safety concerns arising from the availability of ULLMs might prompt a replay of the 1990s when authorities tried to limit the availability of cryptographic code, Lin said, "It is difficult to predict whether model abliteration tools will face similar legal challenges.

"As shown in Section 5.1 of our paper, refusal-direction ablation (i.e., abliteration) appeared in 2024 and quickly gained popularity within the open-source LLM community. Within approximately two years, a growing ecosystem of publicly available tools had emerged to support this technique.

"In the meantime, techniques for both removing and mitigating LLM safety alignment have also become active research topics in academia, with many researchers releasing open-source tools and artifacts to support their studies."

Dealing with the risks posed by uncensored models isn't easy because it depends on divining the intent of the user's prompt. When is a question about terrorism intended as a plan and when is it guidance for writing a thriller? When is a question about hacking intended for theft and when is it cybersecurity education?

The current approach taken by commercial labs — limiting powerful models to favored paying insiders and offering hobbled models to the rest — doesn't work for those left out. Applying some similarly censorious regime to open weight models isn't likely to achieve any more success than efforts by law enforcement to make cryptography available only to "the good guys."
Lin expects that greater transparency, auditability, and verification of models will help.

"As discussed in Section 8 of our paper, our approach to identifying uncensored LLMs relies on publicly available model metadata, such as model cards, to identify models that explicitly disclose their uncensored characteristics," he said. "Our findings demonstrate the value of such transparency for identifying potentially unsafe models.

"Regulatory frameworks have also increasingly emphasized AI documentation and transparency. For example, the EU AI Act requires providers of general-purpose AI models to maintain technical documentation covering model characteristics, capabilities, limitations, and evaluation results. Similarly, the Colorado AI Act recognizes model cards and dataset cards as possible documentation supporting AI impact assessments."
Hugging Face, in the process of being acquired by Nvidia, did not respond to a request for comment. Nor did Kaggle or John Snow Labs, the two other US-based companies named in the study.
According to Lin, the research findings were responsibly disclosed to Hugging Face, John Snow Labs, OpenCSG, Kaggle, ModelScope, and Open Router.

Asked whether any of the companies responded, Lin said, "We received a response from OpenCSG, which expressed appreciation for our work on identifying and measuring uncensored LLMs, stating that 'your research is meaningful and supports the development of a safe and trustworthy LLM ecosystem.'"
OpenCSG, the report says, has committed to enhance its service based on the research findings. ®

74fbfcd64d12556a: In the Guria region, an organization is helping people recover a history the Soviets tried to erase
Originally published on Global Voices
Resort in the Guria region of Georgia. Photo by Tinari.totoro on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Guria is a region in Georgia, situated in the southwestern part of the country. It has a coastline on the Black Sea to the west, which is about 22 kilometers (13 miles) long, and the region is bordered by the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region to the north, Imereti to the east, and the Autonomous Republic of Adjara to the south. It has a rich history and a historical tradition of democracy.
Today, in the region, independent media access is limited and digital literacy remains low. However, Guria has a civic tradition that most of its own residents do not know about in detail.

In 1904, locals organized protests against imperial (Russian, at the time) institutions, formed institutions of self-governance, and proclaimed the Gurian Republic, an early experiment in participatory democracy.

The republic was violently suppressed first by the Russian tsarist empire, and later all the memories of it were fragmented further by decades of deliberate erasure under Soviet occupation of Georgia (1921–1991) and by repressions.
This is exactly what the Digital Spark Spotlight project in Georgia focused on: history and memory in the Guria region.
Global Voices interviewed Lika Mergaladze, head of the organization Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, about their project: what they have done and what they learned through it.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?

Lika Mergaladze (LM): Our organization, Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, works to preserve local history, strengthen civic engagement, and promote sustainable development in the Guria region of Georgia. We use exhibitions, workshops, digital storytelling, and collaborative activities to connect communities with their history and encourage active participation in civic life.

We chose to get involved in the Digital Spark project because we saw an opportunity to combine local history with modern digital technologies. We wanted to help community members document and share their family stories, develop digital skills, and better understand the connection between the past and present. We believe that preserving historical memory and encouraging critical thinking are essential for building an informed and active community.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

LM: One of the main challenges in Guria is that many important historical stories have been forgotten or remain untold. These stories were purposely erased during the Soviet Union. Many families who were the victims of a series of repressions in the 1920s and 30s learned to remain silent about their past in the 50s after World War II. As a result, younger generations often know very little about their ancestors and the region’s democratic traditions, including the Gurian Republic of 1904.

Another challenge is limited access to independent media and low levels of digital literacy in local communities. The dominance of social media and television as information sources makes media literacy and critical thinking particularly important.

We undertook this project to address these challenges by helping local people preserve their history, recognize misinformation and propaganda, and use digital tools to share their stories with a wider audience.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

LM: Through the project ‘From Understanding the Past to the Digital Future,’ implemented from April to October 2026, we organized several activities across the three municipalities of Guria: Ozurgeti, Chokhatauri, and Lanchkhuti. Our main activities included a public discussion. On June 24, we organized ‘What Drove Gurians Crazy? Propaganda Now and Then,’ exploring Guria’s democratic history, Soviet occupation, propaganda, and contemporary challenges. We also did digital storytelling workshops, an AI and Digital Creation workshop and a theatrical performance: on August 12, we presented “My Days and My Father’s Diaries,” dedicated to Meri Chanukvadze and her father, Amberki Chanukvadze, whose life reflected the impact of Soviet repression. These activities helped strengthen participants’ digital skills, encourage historical research, and create opportunities for community members to share their stories online.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

LM: The project generated strong interest across all three municipalities, reaching nearly 50 community members, with particularly strong participation from women and young people. Locals participated in the digital storytelling workshop, including 12 women. These activities gave participants practical opportunities to develop their digital skills and explore new ways of communicating important ideas. Another meaningful example was the theatrical performance dedicated to Meri and her father. More than 35 people attended and participated in a discussion afterwards. The performance encouraged people to reflect on the experiences of families affected by Soviet repression and the importance of preserving historical memory.

The project also laid the foundation for a cross-municipal network of young people, activists, and aspiring digital storytellers. This network can help community members continue documenting local history, sharing civic information, and engaging in public discussions beyond the project itself.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

LM: Our participation in the project strengthened our understanding of how digital technologies can support civic engagement and democratic participation. We gained greater awareness of the importance of digital storytelling, media literacy, and critical thinking in helping communities understand their history and respond to contemporary challenges. We also explored how AI-assisted content creation can provide new opportunities for preserving local stories and making them accessible to wider audiences. The project reinforced our belief that digital tools are not simply communication technologies; they can also help people participate in public life, challenge misinformation, and contribute to community development. Most importantly, we recognized that connecting historical memory with modern digital tools can help create a more informed, active, and engaged society.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

LM: One of the most valuable lessons was that many people are interested in learning about their history when they are given a welcoming space to ask questions and share experiences. Family stories can open up broader conversations about democracy, human rights, repression, and civic responsibility.

We also learned that practical workshops and collaborative activities are effective ways to introduce digital tools to community members. The strong participation of women and young people demonstrated the potential for inclusive, community-based learning.

Another important lesson was the value of combining traditional storytelling with digital technologies. Personal stories, family diaries, public discussions, and theatrical performances can make historical events more relatable and meaningful.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?
LM: We plan to build on the experience and connections developed through the project by continuing to document, digitize, and share historical and civic stories from Guria.

We aim to encourage more community members, especially young people and women, to use digital storytelling and online content creation to preserve family histories and discuss local issues. We also intend to apply the knowledge gained from the workshops to future educational activities, community discussions, and collaborative initiatives.

An important priority will be to strengthen the network of local journalists, activists, and digital storytellers across Ozurgeti, Chokhatauri, and Lanchkhuti. By supporting collaboration and knowledge-sharing, we hope to ensure that these activities continue beyond the project period.
Written by Daria Dergacheva

19d132bfd53eb32c: From MyPower Corporation

As delegates gathered in Vienna, Austria, for the 70th International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) general conference, geopolitical tensions continued to show how events thousands of kilometres away can disrupt energy markets, supply chains and fuel prices.
These are very different challenges, but they remind us of something Malaysia cannot take for granted: resilience and energy security.
How do we ensure that our electricity system remains reliable, secure and cost-competitive as demand grows, while also moving towards cleaner energy?
There is no simple answer, and no single technology can meet every need. Nuclear energy is one of the options Malaysia is examining, and this is not our first time doing so.

Malaysia joined the IAEA on Jan 15, 1969 as its 101st member. Over five decades later, the agency has grown to more than 180 member states, reflecting the expanding role of nuclear science and technology around the world.

For Malaysia, nuclear technology has never been solely about electricity generation. Nuclear science at the domestic scene is always about supporting peaceful applications in areas such as medicine, agriculture, industry, research and environmental monitoring.

We have explored nuclear power before. Earlier efforts included feasibility studies and the establishment of the Malaysia Nuclear Power Corporation (MNPC) in 2011 as the country's nuclear energy programme implementing organisation. That programme did not ultimately proceed as planned.
Today's assessment therefore does not mean Malaysia is starting from zero. Neither is it simply reviving an earlier project. We are revisiting the nuclear question, but in a very different world.

In tandem with the nation's economic growth, electricity demand is also growing. Data centres and new industries are intensely changing the shape of future demand growth. As Malaysia moves towards a cleaner energy system, energy security has become increasingly important amid geopolitical uncertainty.

Malaysia is not alone in taking time to consider nuclear power. Bangladesh first explored the Rooppur project in the 1960s, but construction only began decades later in 2017. Turkey also made several attempts before the construction of its first nuclear power plant at Akkuyu began in 2018. Many other countries have also taken long journeys towards nuclear power.

Closer to home, Vietnam has revived its nuclear power development plan and has requested an IAEA Phase 2 Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review mission, while the Philippines is also moving forward with preparations for a nuclear power programme.
Their experiences show that the path to nuclear power is rarely straightforward. Countries may pause, reassess and adjust plans as national priorities and circumstances change.

Their experiences do not mean Malaysia should follow the same path. Every country has its circumstances. They simply remind us that nuclear programmes rarely move in a straight line. Governments change, economies progress, technology develops and national priorities evolve.

That was the broader context for Malaysia's participation in the IAEA conference from Sept 14 to 18. The scale of the gathering is significant. The IAEA brings together more than 180 member states, and 36 ministers attended this year's conference alongside senior officials, regulators, scientists and representatives of international organisations.

Malaysia's delegation was headed by the energy transition and water transformation ministry (Petra) secretary-general, with representatives from the Malaysian permanent mission in Vienna, Malaysian Nuclear Agency, atomic energy department and MyPower Corporation.

Malaysia delivered its national statement, sharing the country's progress in the peaceful uses of nuclear science and technology, and the work under way to assess the possible role of nuclear energy in electricity generation.

Malaysia has also been elected to serve on the IAEA governors board for 2026-2028, giving it a greater role in the agency's governance and discussions on nuclear safety, security, safeguards, peaceful uses and international cooperation.
The general conference, bilateral meetings and side events provide a platform for countries to exchange experiences across the much wider world of nuclear science and technology.

A key highlight of Malaysia's engagement in Vienna was the bilateral meeting with IAEA director-general Rafael Mariano Grossi, which reaffirmed the importance of international cooperation in strengthening national nuclear infrastructure.
Malaysia shared its ongoing preparations and plans for an Integrated INIR Phase 1 mission to independently assess progress and identify areas for improvement.

For Malaysia, the priority is not deciding when to build a nuclear power plant, but ensuring that the country has the knowledge, institutions and capabilities to make an informed decision. Malaysia remains in Phase 1 of the IAEA milestones approach, with no firm decision yet on nuclear power deployment, technology, vendor or site.

Malaysians will understandably have questions. Is nuclear safe? How much will it cost? What happens to radioactive waste? Who pays for the plant and its eventual decommissioning? Are our institutions ready?
These are fair questions. They deserve clear answers. Studying nuclear does not mean advocating for it. Equally, we should not dismiss an option before understanding what it can, and cannot, offer.

Renewable energy will remain central to Malaysia's energy transition. But our challenge is broader than adding renewable capacity. We must also consider what the electricity system will need as demand grows and the role of coal declines.

The haze during the week of the conference was a visible reminder of our environmental challenges. Geopolitical uncertainty offers another reminder that energy security and resilience matter, too. There is no single technology that solves every problem.
Malaysia's presence in Vienna should therefore not be read as a signal that we have already chosen nuclear power. It means we are preparing to make an informed choice.
The IAEA can provide expertise, international experience and independent peer review. Countries that have travelled on this road can tell us what worked and, just as importantly, what did not.

Ultimately, the decision belongs to Malaysia. Our task today is not to rush towards a reactor but to ask difficult questions, develop our people, strengthen our institutions and understand the responsibilities involved.
For something that could shape Malaysia's energy system for generations, doing the homework first is not a delay. It is simply a pertinent process and a responsible action.
MyPower Corporation is the government agency coordinating electricity sector reforms and nuclear power planning.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

27adac5be6a25903: Grand Theft Auto VI may put a dent in global productivity today but the game didn’t break the internet.

For those unfamiliar, GTA VI is the first new instalment of the mega-hit game in 13 years and it is nearly impossible to understate the excitement surrounding its release. Anecdotal evidence suggests fans of the game may today report they suddenly feel unfit to perform paid work.
Developer Rockstar Games allowed Xbox and PlayStation owners to pay for and download the 200GB-plus game on November 10, before play commenced on the 19th.

Millions took advantage of the chance to download the game, creating just the sort of internet traffic event that regional internet registry the Réseaux IP Européens Network Coordination Centre (RIPE NCC) can observe with its RIPE Atlas internet measurement network.
RIPE data scientist Emile Aben, with help from staffers Alun Davies and James Cowie, went looking for GTA-related traffic and found some interesting patterns.

Aben observed that traffic to PlayStations mostly came from content delivery networks operated by AWS and Fastly. Microsoft relied on Fastly for over half of traffic flowing to Xboxes and used Akamai too, but eschewed AWS's CloudFront.

The data scientist observed heavy use of “GeoDNS,” a technique that returns different IP addresses for a single domain request, depending on a user’s location. DNS’s designers didn’t intend that. Indeed, the RIPE trio point out that Paul Vixie, the computer scientist who earned his place in the Internet Hall of Fame for massive contributions to the DNS system, regarded things like GeoDNS as “stupid DNS tricks.”
Whatever you think of GeoDNS, the RIPE researchers found that folks who were likely downloading GTA VI from Los Angeles, Tokyo, and Istanbul were each directed to different sites.
Their probe of a network in Shanghai, China, found “a very distinct long lookup-chain with a hostname that is associated with the Alibaba Cloud in the end that maps to six different IP addresses.”
“This hints at specialised treatment for some countries/regions,” Aben wrote.

He also noted that Internet Exchange Points, the interconnect facilities that network operators use to exchange traffic and shorten paths, had to cope with record traffic during the download period – and seem to have handled the load.
Aben thinks the GTA VI download program offers a useful lesson.

“DNS helps steer each player towards a download server, while multiple CDNs share the work of delivering the files,” he wrote. “That distribution matters beyond gaming. On the open Internet, game downloads share routers and link capacity with all kinds of other traffic, including critical services.”
“Keeping downloads local helps leave capacity on long-distance links free for other uses, making that enormous demand manageable.” ®

e5d8c3d4efd94fea: Burak Kara/GettyThis week, it was revealed that 100 corporations and industry groups tied to fossil fuel interests – including the US multinational ExxonMobil and French energy company TotalEnergies – have sent delegations to this year’s global climate summit COP31 in Turkey. These climate talks have a long history of lobbyist interference. More than 1,600 fossil fuel lobbyists attended the COP30 talks in Brazil last year, and more than 1,700 at the 2024 talks in Azerbaijan. This is a problem. The whole point of these long-running United Nations negotiations is to address human-caused climate change, which is primarily driven by burning oil, gas and coal – the very products these lobbyists are paid to promote. At COP31, fossil lobbyists will have been hard at work promoting fossil fuels. Their methods often draw on what academics call “discourses of delay”. This is how it works. To slow the shift away from fossil fuels, lobbyists spread disinformation, such as claiming fossil fuels are part of the solution (“gas is a transition fuel”), that future technologies will save us (carbon capture), or we’re doomed and it’s too late to act. Oil and gas companies have dramatically increased their Google ads in the month leading up to COP31, for example. Researchers have shown fossil fuel lobbyists use a two-pronged strategy. First, they point to a lack of international action as a reason for not acting on climate change at home. Second, they work to stymie progress at the same international talks. A new UN report says it’s now too late to hold the global temperature rise to 1.5°C. The world will likely pass this threshold in 2030. A big reason for this is obstruction by lobbyists of climate policies that target the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. So, why are fossil fuel lobbyists allowed into these talks? Pushback in Brazil At last year’s COP30 summit, host country Brazil tried to push back against fossil fuel lobbyists. Alongside the UN and UNESCO, Brazil launched an international partnership to counter climate change disinformation and misinformation. Thirty countries have since signed onto the declaration, which calls out the: growing impact of disinformation, misinformation, denialism […] and other tactics used to undermine the integrity of information on climate change, which diminish public understanding, delay urgent action, and threaten the global climate response and societal stability. Lobbyists gain access to the talks in different ways, including through affiliations with non-governmental organisations and industry groups and as part of official government delegations. While this year’s draft negotiating text makes reference to information integrity, there’s still no clear code of conduct or meaningful disclosure of fossil fuel industry ties for the thousands of delegates attending COP31. There are no clear, explicit rules against spreading climate disinformation. COP30 President Andre Correa do Lago (centre) listens to his advisers at the conference in Brazil last year. Brazil has since produced a global roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. Pablo Porciuncula/Getty A long history of lobbying Sadly, this story is all too familiar. For as long as there have been international climate talks, fossil fuel lobbyists have tried to persuade countries not to act with the urgency the science demands. It took more than a quarter of a century of climate talks before fossil fuels were explicitly addressed at the Glasgow COP in 2021. Until then, the focus was on greenhouse gas emissions – but not the fossil fuels causing them. Corporate fossil fuel lobbyists have been assisted by so-called petrostates, such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, whose economies are highly dependent on oil and gas production. And when the oil- and gas-producing states Azerbaijan and the United Arab Emirates hosted the COP talks in 2023 and 2024, respectively, both countries used the summit to push new fossil fuel deals. What are lobbyists targeting this time? There are more than 100 different agenda items up for debate at COP31, many of which are opposed by fossil fuel lobbyists. Negotiators are still discussing a UN initiative designed to rapidly increase efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, for instance. Alongside the official agenda, COP President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum released a separate “action” agenda organised around ten themes. Some of these, such as transitioning to clean energy, threaten fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel lobbyists will likely try to block calls for phasing out coal, gas and oil – just as they did last year, where Brazil’s efforts to formalise a roadmap transitioning away from fossil fuels ran aground. Another concern for fossil fuel interests is the electrification goal, aimed at boosting electricity’s global share of final energy demand to 35% by 2035. If this translates to more electric vehicles, batteries and heat pumps in homes and electric furnaces in factories, it would mean less demand for oil and gas. That would affect profits for companies such as ExxonMobil and Shell. Australia on the tightrope Australian Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen is acting as president of negotiations at COP31 as part of a co-hosting arrangement with Turkey (also known as Turkiye). This represents a tightrope walk for Australia. Domestically, the Albanese Labor government is attempting to speed up the energy transition. Policies such as subsidising home batteries have proven a strong success. More than 600,000 households have installed batteries since the program began last year. Electric vehicle uptake is rapidly accelerating. Internationally, however, Australia remains one of the world’s largest coal and gas exporters. State and federal governments keep approving new projects. Given this, many countries have questioned Australia’s climate credibility, especially its Pacific neighbours. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was heavily criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his opening COP31 speech. Just minutes before Albanese spoke, UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged countries to make fossil fuels “go the way of the dinosaurs”. “The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do,” he said. Can progress be made despite lobbyists? As COP31 enters its final days, the eyes of the world will be on Australia and Turkey. Should the co-hosts fail to get agreement on concrete steps to advance Brazil’s latest efforts to transition away from fossil fuels, many countries will be left disappointed. But despite the best efforts of the fossil fuel industry, momentum for a shift away from oil, gas and coal is gathering pace outside the UN talks. In April, nations attended the first international conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels, while the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative continues to gain members. As always, though, much more needs to be done, and quickly. Clamping down on lobbyists and climate misinformation is well overdue. Christian Downie receives funding from the Australian Research Council. William Kakenmaster receives funding from the Australian Research Council.
e18b15495b2ebaa3: At 08:30 on Thursday morning every powered-on mobile phone in South Korea blared out an Extreme Emergency Alert tone for 10.5 seconds – but the nation was at peace, with no major natural disasters occurring.

Korean media report the 08:30 alert turned up nine phones.
Authorities will send a second alert tone at an unspecified time later in the day to again smoke out any surreptitious smartphones.

It’s not possible to opt out of the alerts, one reason a concerned netizen has used the Android issue tracker to suggest sending alerts to detect exam cheats could be an abuse of the emergency alert system that Google might want to do something about.

South Korea sends a lot of emergency alerts, for matters such as helping to find missing persons or to warn of dangerous weather. It’s not uncommon to receive several in a single day. Authorities also gave advance notice of the CSAT alerts, which will not, therefore, cause panic on the streets of Seoul or Busan.
CSAT day is, however, a serious occasion. Some businesses open late so test-takers can get to their exams without having to battle peak hour traffic.
Those measures are arguably less disruptive than the widespread internet outages that some states in India impose on major exam days.

An alleged leak of one Indian exam paper saw the nation’s tech regulator ban messaging service Telegram in the country and eventually sparked a youth protest movement that New Delhi tried to suppress with more deliberate internet outages. ®
24abcf689c6b9b5d: From Terence Netto
Former Sarawak DAP vice-chairman Wong King Wei has advised DAP to stay out of the Dec 12 Sarawak polls, citing the need for DAP to be friendly with the idea of state autonomy for Sarawakian parties.
Sarawakians want to assert the interests of their state after years of deferring to federal interests.
Decades-old reticence about their interests has in recent years been replaced by an assertiveness that Putrajaya cannot but respect.
The intensive battle between competing political coalitions in the peninsula makes the courtship of Sarawakian (and Sabahan) political parties imperative.
These days, the keys to Putrajaya, for peninsula aspirants, lie between Kuching and Kota Kinabalu.

Since the major Sarawakian parties have banded together into a fairly cohesive force in Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS), it does not make sense for DAP to be at cross-purposes with GPS components in the upcoming state polls.
As a single party, DAP may well emerge with the highest or second highest number of parliamentary seats in the next general election (GE16), which is due by February 2028.
No single party or coalition is expected to gain a simple majority in GE16.
This will require one or the other coalition in the peninsula to importune GPS to back them for the right to form the federal government.

DAP, as the anticipated holder of a sizeable number of seats in the peninsula, will be critical to negotiations with GPS, which is expected to sweep not only the state seats in the Dec 12 polls but also the parliamentary ones in GE16.
After seeing how the peninsula Malay vote is solidifying behind Umno and PAS-led Perikatan Nasional, DAP must think strategically about GE16.

Based on their performance in the Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka polls, DAP's Pakatan Harapan (PH) allies PKR and Amanah are struggling to make a dent in the Malay vote, and are no more confident of the non-Malay vote bank.
Fear of the evolving collaboration between Umno and PAS will keep the Chinese vote with DAP despite discomfort with DAP’s overly compliant attitude towards Anwar Ibrahim.

DAP secretary-general Loke Siew Fook, presently unencumbered by ministerial duties, will have more time to espouse the reforms championed by PH that have been neglected by Anwar's puzzling pussyfooting.
The path is open to a de facto premiership by Loke – by careful rhetoric and subtle gesture – given Anwar's continued tepidity in pursuing the reformasi agenda.
Nuanced rhetoric and statesmanlike gestures by Loke can restrain Sarawak DAP leader Chong Chieng Jen from remonstrating against a DAP decision to refrain from contesting in the Sarawak polls.

DAP should also signal to Rafizi Ramli’s Bersama to be realistic about its chances in GE16, which will require the PKR splinter to go only for the parliamentary seats – 10 at the most – that the Rafizi claque in PKR can win in GE16.
After two underwhelming outings in Johor and Melaka, Bersama ought to come down from the clouds and see that there is no point in overrating its chances.

So, it’s a rearguard action that DAP must undertake, running into GE16, to save what can be salvaged from the growing wreck of Anwar's myopia and Amanah’s failure to convince the Malays that moderate Islam is not a delusion but a viable proposition.
It’s the high road that beckons DAP which also happens to be the pragmatic road to take in the circumstances.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.

000c7eec3c44d2c9: Saya kira jika kita bercakap mengenai Umno yang berusaha di Negeri Sembilan untuk membetulkan keadaan bodoh yang mereka sendiri ceburi, kita akan menepuk dahi berkali-kali. Umno dan PAS tidak rajin membaca, dan belajar.

Oleh sebab yang menderhaka di Negeri Sembilan itu ada dalam kalangan mereka adalah Adun daripada PAS, saya ingin membawa pembaca PAS ke negeri Terengganu. Ini kerana Terengganu adalah negeri solid PAS. Terengganu juga adalah negeri presiden PAS. Justeru, dalam banyak keadaan Terengganu ada tempat istimewa dalam kepala ahli PAS. Leluhur Tuanku Aishah Rohani, iaitu Tuanku Ampuan Besar Negeri Sembilan berasal dari Terengganu. Nenda baginda Tuanku Aishah adalah Haji Su Mahmud (juga dikenali sebagai Che Su Mahmud). Haji Su adalah anak kepada menteri besar Terengganu yang pertama, iaitu Ngah Muhammad Yusof yang berasal dan bertapak di Kampung Batu Burok, Kuala Terengganu. Ibu Haji Su adalah Cik Teh Fatimah Ali.

Haji Su Mahmud dipandang terhormat di Terengganu yang mana sebelum kematiannya pada tahun 1940, beliau telah mewakafkan kediamannya untuk menjadi bangunan Sekolah Menengah Agama (Atas) Sultan Zainal Abidin (SMAASZA). Beliau juga adalah bekas pegawai daerah di Kuala Berang ketika pendudukan Jepun.

Anak perempuan Haji Su iaitu Zainun-Mariam binti Haji Su Mahmud, berkahwin dengan kerabat Terengganu, dan merupakan bonda kepada Tuanku Aishah Rohani (Duli Yang Maha Mulia Tunku Ampuan Besar Negeri Sembilan). Ayahanda Tuanku Aishah Rohani adalah Almarhum Tengku Besar Mahmud (Tengku Seri Utama Raja Tengku Besar Mahmud Sultan Zainal Abidin III Terengganu). Dalam erti kata lain, Tuanku Ampuan Negeri Sembilan adalah cucunda kepada Sultan Terengganu iaitu Almarhum Sultan Zainal Abidin III, merangkap cucu kepada menteri besar Terengganu.

Memahami nasab dan leluhur Tuanku Aishah baik dari jalur ayahanda atau bondanya ini sangat penting. Ini kerana baginda merupakan anakanda saudara kepada tiga orang Sultan Terengganu iaitu Almarhum Sultan Haji Muhammad II Muadzam Shah, Almarhum Sultan Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah, dan Almarhum Sultan Ismail Nasiruddin yang merupakan Yang di-Pertuan Agong keempat. Ini juga menjadikan baginda Tuanku Aishah Rohani bonda saudara kepada Sultan Terengganu iaitu Sultan Mizan Zainal Abidin dan juga bonda saudara kepada Raja Perempuan Perlis Tuanku Fauziah Tengku Abdul Rashid yang merupakan cucunda kepada Sultan Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah.

Keadaan ini juga meletakkan Tuanku Aishah Rohani sebagai sepupu kepada Almarhum Sultanah Asma Sultan Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah yang merupakan bonda tiri kepada Almarhum Tuanku Abdul Halim Mu'adzam Shah dan bonda kepada Sultan Kedah, Sultan Sallehuddin Sultan Badlishah. Sekali gus menjadikan baginda berpangkat bonda saudara kepada Sultan Sallehuddin.

Dalam konteks orang Melayu, dan adatnya, status anak gahara atau anak raja yang lahir daripada pasangan yang kedua-duanya berdarah diraja atau bangsawan sangatlah mustahak dipertimbangkan. Dalam hal melibatkan pewarisan takhta, anak gahara dianggap mempunyai jurai keturunan yang paling tulen. Justeru, mereka akan sentiasa diberikan keutamaan mutlak untuk menaiki takhta atau dilantik sebagai putera mahkota berbanding anak raja yang ibunya daripada orang kebanyakan (atau bukan berdarah raja). Hal ini adalah untuk mengelakkan konflik di mana pelantikan waris yang bukan anak gahara sering ditentang oleh kerabat diraja atau pembesar negeri. Ia juga merupakan petunjuk kepada keabsahan selain menjadi simbol kedaulatan.

Di Negeri Sembilan soal status anak gahara pernah sekali sahaja tidak dipertimbangkan. Kita faham sistem beraja di Negeri Sembilan mengamalkan sistem pemilihan oleh Undang Yang Empat. Ini misalnya terlihat setelah Almarhum Tuanku Munawir (anak gahara) mangkat pada tahun 1967, Undang Yang Empat ketika itu telah sebulat suara memilih Tuanku Ja'afar (bukan anak gahara) untuk menaiki takhta sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan ke-10. Tambahan pula usia anakanda Tuanku Munawir (yakni Tuanku Muhriz yang merupakan anak gahara) masih muda.

Namun demikian saya tetap percaya jurai anak gahara ini penting dalam masyarakat Melayu terutama apabila berlaku perselisihan menentukan siapakah yang lebih absah menjadi raja. Atas sebab itulah maka takhta Yamtuan Besar dikembalikan kepada jurai Tuanku Muhriz. Jurai yang ‘terbonam’ pula meletakkan keadaan menjadi rumit.

Seperti telah ditunjukkan, Tuanku Aishah Rohani mempunyai keterserlahan jurai baginda dengan cara tersendiri. Baginda bukan sahaja melengkapkan suaminya, Tuanku Muhriz, tetapi menjadikan kedudukan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan itu istimewa dengan cara unik. Bukan sahaja kehadiran baginda itu meletakkan Negeri Sembilan bertaut dengan keluarga diraja negeri lain, hari ini bahkan baginda adalah bonda kepada dua daripada empat Putera Berempat Negeri Sembilan. Mereka adalah Tunku Besar Seri Menanti Tunku Ali Redhauddin Tuanku Muhriz; dan Tunku Panglima Besar Tunku Zain Al-'Abidin Tuanku Muhriz. Pemilihan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan mendatang akan dipilih oleh Undang yang sah hari ini daripada Putera Empat.

Makanya, jawapan saya kepada pelajar saya memang valid dan relevan; bahawa ahli Umno dan PAS mesti terus membaca agar pandai. Malulah sudah diundi rakyat tetapi masih bebal. Supaya kita yang sedikit cerdik ini tidak menepuk dahi seraya mendecit ‘ayoyo atau haiya’ melihatkan tingkah laku mereka. Ini kerana dari segi Adat Perpatih, mahupun pertimbangan Adat Temenggung (disokong isterinya), Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir beroleh markah penuh.

254fb2fb91acd553: The USA’s new ban on Chinese companies remotely accessing GPUs will have short-term impact, but ultimately see China accelerate its development of domestic alternatives, according to Martin Lau, the president of Chinese web giant Tencent.
Speaking on the company’s Q3 earnings call, Lau said the new US regulation will have an “unfortunate” impact on Tencent’s business.

“It does set everyone back. It sets everyone back in China,” Lau said. “So everyone is actually having less advanced compute to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China.”
He said the ban will impact Tencent’s ability to train models.
“Our training efficiency with Hy4 is actually very high,” he said. “When we look at the next version, it would take probably longer time for us to come up with the next version in the short run.”
“But over time, the domestic supply chain would actually come on board.”
Lau also thinks the bans won’t hamper Tencent’s ability to run inferencing workloads, because made-in-China chips “should be able to cover it.”

“And over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we see the industry is progressing very fast,” he added. “With the latest restriction, we expect it to actually speed up even further, because all the development effort would actually have to be focused on speeding up the domestic supply chain.”

Tencent needs GPUs, and lots of them, because the 10 million users of its agentic assistant WorkBuddy are collectively consuming over 100 trillion tokens per day. Lau thinks WorkBuddy is on track to becoming a hit product, partly because many users are outside China.

Lau said Tencent can serve WorkBuddy customers outside China because the service can operate with different models, and the company thinks it can find third parties to provide the necessary inferencing services without the new US bans creating a problem.
But Lau said that GPU rentals and other cloud services, which are also growing strongly, may be impacted.

“In terms of cloud, if it is non-GPU related, we can actually build capacities ourselves outside of China,” he said. “I think there is still a lot of such opportunities because our cloud service is actually very cost competitive. When it comes to GPU, then unfortunately, we cannot actually offer high-end GPU anymore. We may be able to work with some partners in different places.”

Tencent doesn’t break out revenue for its cloud services, but said they rose by 35 percent year-on-year, well ahead of the company’s overall eight percent growth. Marketing services also grew strongly, by 19 percent, thanks in part to new AI-powered systems that improve ad targeting.
The company’s WeChat and Weixin messaging platforms continued to grow, adding 35 million accounts to exiting the quarter with 1.44 billion monthly active users.
One Tencent biz that went backwards was its international gaming unit, which saw revenue fall nine percent.

Chief strategy officer James Mitchell said that slowdown wasn’t caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. “I think that in fairness, the slowdown for us predated the run-up to GTA VI,” he said, before predicting that Tencent’s existing and future “evergreen games” should help to turn things around.
“The game environment globally is one where the rate of innovation has slowed somewhat, and now with AI, there’s opportunities to re-accelerate innovation,” he said. ®
2baef697661cb837: Dari kemelut tidak ada exco dan tak boleh buka persidangan Adun, membawa pula kepada kekalutan nama calon menteri besar baharu dikemuka kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar ketika menteri besar masih bertugas.

Kalau kita dengar penjelasan pengulas politik popular, Iswardy Morni, akan ada suatu naratif tentang the story behind the drama yang semacam menyokong hujah-hujah beliau. Saya tak mahu ulang di sini, tuan-tuan boleh pergi ke saluran YouTube beliau.

Saya doakan selamat untuk semua ahli politik terlibat dan mengharapkan suatu happy ending -- they all serve the rakyat with great service ever after.
