528841cbf861a044: Most staples for Thanksgiving, including potatoes and cranberries, haven't jumped in price this year. Noah Samuel Franz on UnsplashInflation-weary Americans have at least some good news to cheer this holiday season: The cost of a basic Thanksgiving meal has stabilized. A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people clocks in at US$78.93, approximately 0.4% less than in 2025, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute. That’s because most staples haven’t seen a sharp jump in prices. Americans are still justified in feeling stressed about high grocery bills, but it’s because of the cumulative effect of rising prices in recent years. While inflation has slowed since its peak of more than 9% in 2022, the cost of a Thanksgiving meal is roughly 25% higher than it was before the COVID-19 pandemic began. I’m an agricultural economist who has been studying the many drivers of food inflation. What’s key to remember is that inflation data tells us how quickly prices are increasing, not whether prices are returning to previous levels. So even modest price jumps today are layered on already-elevated prices. Here’s what Americans can expect when they go shopping for Thanksgiving, from turkey to dessert: Go for frozen turkey Stable frozen turkey prices have played an important role in keeping overall holiday meal costs close to last year’s levels. The average advertised price for a frozen turkey over 16 pounds (about 7 kilograms) was $0.96 per pound, essentially unchanged from the $0.97 per pound in the same period last year, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Turkey Report, published on Nov. 13, 2026. These prices reflect the typical discounts leading up to Thanksgiving, when retailers often cut turkey prices as part of their holiday promotions. It’s a different story with fresh turkey prices, which are about 11% higher than a year ago, according to the Department of Agriculture data. So shoppers seeking a fresh bird may face a higher grocery bill. A longer-term trend is that turkey consumption has gradually declined over time. As a result, the cost of Thanksgiving depends on much more than turkey prices alone. This is where side dishes come in. Frozen turkey is among the Thanksgiving staples that haven’t seen big price jumps this past year. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh A mixed picture for side dishes Mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce and sweet potato casserole are among the dishes that a frugal shopper might consider. Sweet potatoes are 12.5% cheaper year on year, and cranberry prices have dropped 4.8%, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Grocery Store Specialty Crops data. Potato prices, meanwhile, have been stable, increasing just 1.1% over the past year, according to September’s consumer price index, the most recent month of full data. If you’re considering mac and cheese, the costs of the main ingredients should balance out: Pasta and cornmeal prices are 4.3% higher year on year, while cheese is 3% cheaper. Prices for fruits and vegetables, however, have mostly ticked upward and are 3.9% higher than a year ago. That includes green beans, which are 2.2% more expensive. Prices for fresh apples are up 7.5%, and up 2.6% for lettuce. More broadly, higher prices for some fresh vegetables reflect the cost pressures facing food production. Farmers are grappling with high fertilizer, fuel and transportation expenses, not to mention tariffs in certain sectors. Of course, Thanksgiving isn’t complete without regional traditions. Sauerkraut is a popular side dish for turkey in the mid-Atlantic states, but fans will have to pay substantially more. Cabbage is about 30% more expensive year on year due to weather shocks and pest outbreaks that have reduced supply. Sauerkraut, a popular side dish in mid-Atlantic states, is likely to be pricier amid higher cabbage prices. Kelsey Todd on Unsplash Don’t forget dessert Americans might also find some sweet relief in prices for popular desserts. Some key baking staples became more affordable. Butter prices have fallen 10.3% over the previous year, while flour is down by 1.1% and sugar by 1%, according to the September consumer price index data. But some of the biggest savings come from eggs, where prices have dropped sharply. Like the turkey industry, egg production was hard-hit in 2022 by a highly pathogenic avian flu outbreak, which reduced supplies and pushed prices up. Since then, producers have rebuilt flocks and expanded production to grow supply. Egg prices are now 20.3% lower than a year ago. Where consumers will shell out more is milk, up 2.3%; canned fruit, up 2.3%; and frozen bakery products, up 1.3%, according to the consumer price index data. Pumpkins for pie-making will cost 2% more than last year. So keep all this in mind if you plan to bake a pie. And if you opt for a store-bought pumpkin pie, expect to pay about 2.5% more. Where other savings can be found Shoppers looking for alternatives to turkey could head to the poultry aisle. Prices for whole fryer and roaster chickens are anywhere from 7% to 20% lower than a year ago, according to USDA grocery store price data. Consumers can also take advantage of Thanksgiving promotions offered by grocery retailers. Several major retailers offer complete Thanksgiving meal baskets for less than $40, which can translate to approximately $3.50 to $4 per person. Among major retailers, Walmart is advertising its Thanksgiving basket for 10 people at $35, Aldi at $39 for 10 people and Target at $30 for six people. Although the contents vary, these meal packages generally include Thanksgiving favorites such as turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce, and ingredients for green bean and potato side dishes. Inflation remains at the top of consumers’ minds, and it isn’t expected to ease anytime soon. But in the case of Thanksgiving, shoppers can find at least some relief as they seek out staples for their feast. Elizabeth Canales receives funding from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
62b49bc7f7abf6f9: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s

In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver.
How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us?
—Amit Katwala
Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region’s two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure.
Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power.
—Casey Crownhart
MIT Technology Review Narrated: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom

Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.

As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.

IVF has brought millions of babies into the world over the last four decades. But the process can still be slow, painful, and expensive—and far from guaranteed to work. Now, a wave of new technologies aims to change that.

df0acd98824586e8: BANGKOK, Nov 18 — Chemicals found almost everywhere in modern life pose a “global and growing threat” to human health and the environment, a landmark report based on over a decade of research has warned. The report on “endocrine-disrupting chemicals” (EDCs) released by the United Nations Environment Programme and World Health Organization “conservatively” estimates the health and environmental costs of EDC exposure at over US$1 trillion (RM4.1 trillion) annually. “The scientific evidence is clear: EDCs are a global and growing threat to human and environmental health,” warns the report written by international scientists, calling current regulations “uneven and insufficient.” EDCs are chemicals that interfere with, mimic, or block the hormones that regulate the development and behaviour of our organs. They are in everything from toys and makeup, to building materials and clothing. The report released late Tuesday is the first such comprehensive look at EDC impacts in 14 years, and finds increasingly clear links between them and a range of diseases. “The evidence is so strong that it’s irrefutable at this point,” said Laura Vandenberg, report co-author and professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. The report examined thousands of studies on chemicals like bisphenols, phthalates and parabens. Evidence of links between these chemicals and disease is strongest for certain neurological conditions and reproductive problems including sperm decline. But there is also growing confidence that EDCs are linked to diseases like type 2 diabetes and asthma that have spiked globally. “Because these changes are occurring rapidly, they are unlikely to be explained primarily by genetic change,” the report says. ‘Sufficiently worrisome’ Scientists looked at associations between EDC exposure and health conditions, as well as the mechanisms by which exposure could cause harm. The findings vary, with “strong evidence” of developmental and neurobehavioral effects, but “emerging” links between EDCs and cardiovascular disease. However, the overall risk is strong because EDCs are so ubiquitous and likely to impact health at tiny levels, Vandenberg said. Among those most at risk are workers in the chemicals and recycling industries, particularly in countries with weak regulations. A 2024 study by the International Pollutants Elimination Network NGO fitted participants with silicone wristbands that absorbed chemicals. Lab tests of the wristbands found that plastic waste and recycling workers in Thailand and Kenya were exposed to over 20 hazardous chemicals, while even control subjects working in offices were exposed to at least 11. There are around 1,000 identified EDCs, but experts say many chemicals have simply not been tested properly and their impacts remain unknown. They are also concerned about “synergistic” impacts — the way exposure to multiple chemicals may amplify health effects. The “proverbial million-dollar question” is what level of EDC exposure triggers any given health impact, said Frederic Leusch, professor of environmental toxicology at Australia’s Griffith University, who was not involved in the report. But even absent an answer, Leusch believes “the hazard is sufficiently worrisome that we need to take action to reduce our, and our environment’s, exposure.” ‘It scares politicians’ Many countries have regulated certain EDCs, often targeting bisphenol A, particularly in children’s products. But regulators have struggled to determine which chemicals should be regulated, and what an appropriate exposure level might be. “It scares politicians, to some extent, because it’s such a complicated area,” said retired professor of environmental chemistry Ake Bergman, who worked on the previous editions of the EDC report in 2002 and 2012. Like other experts, he warned there is no known safe exposure level for most EDCs. “We have some that are really acting at extremely low concentrations.” In a statement, the International Council of Chemical Associations industry group called for “science-based” approaches to regulation that protect health and the environment “while enabling society to benefit from the products, technologies, and innovations that are essential to modern life and sustainable development.” Many EDCs are in plastics, and experts say oil firms are increasing plastic production as demand for fossil fuel energy falls. “We need to stop the expansion of plastic production,... reduce exposures to EDCs, and ban the worst actors,” said Tracey Woodruff, report co-author and professor at Stanford University. “While more science is always needed, we don’t need more science to act.” — AFP

69c36030a7446a10: PARIS، Nov 18 —After 13 years of waiting، including two delays and several leaks، the first gamers began playing Wednesday the latest instalment of Grand Theft Auto، the most expensive — and among the most profitable — video game ever developed. GTA VI becomes available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series consoles at midnight Thursday in each region where it will be available. That meant it launched first in New Zealand (at 1100 GMT on Wednesday)، with many players around the world changing their console location settings to the far-eastern country to be among the first to enter the new Vice City. “I’ve been playing GTA for such a long time that the anticipation for this is crazy، ” Australian student Riley Fennel told AFP ahead of the launch. Although Rockstar Games، the studio behind GTA، has not yet released advance unit sales figures، specialist firm Sensor Tower estimates they have already surpassed 15 million. That would be more than US$1.5 billion (RM6.17 billion) in revenue before the game even came out، for a budget estimated at US$1 billion to US$1.5 billion، which would be unprecedented. According to the British analytics firm Omdia، sales of GTA VI could reach US$3.2 billion by the end of the year. ‘Taylor Swift of games’ “No other concert or box office release has ever generated that much capital. And so that makes it one of the outliers in entertainment، ” said Joost van Dreunen، a professor at New York University’s Stern School of Business. “This is the Taylor Swift of video games، ” the industry specialist said. Rockstar’s parent company، US publisher Take-Two Interactive، has rolled out a massive marketing campaign to establish the title as a mass cultural product that transcends the boundaries of video games. “The reach of the game is such that it will lead to a downstream effect on engagement on other entertainment services، ” such as streaming platforms، said James McWhirter at Omdia. “I’m going to take four days off، ” said Dmytro Shkambara، a 27-year-old Ukrainian player living in Berlin، who said he had been planning this first game session “for a very long time”. Like him، many fans have already booked time off to immerse themselves in the fictional state of Leonida، inspired by Florida. The human resources platform Remote said it had seen a 32 percent increase in leave requests around the world for November 19. Touted as bigger، better and more realistic than its predecessors، “GTA VI” follows the adventures of a Bonnie-and-Clyde-style couple trying to survive in the Miami-inspired، crime-ravaged Vice City. Since its beginnings، the series has won players over with its increasingly realistic reconstructions of fictionalised cities and the great freedom of action offered in a highly detailed open world. Gamers entering GTA’s worlds can drive cars، fly planes or go skydiving. “GTA VI” promises to push its realism even further، with characters looking different depending on what they eat and players having to work at cultivating the relationship between the protagonists. Ahead of its release، the game picked up eight nominations on Tuesday at the Game Awards، the American ceremony that will honour the best video games of the year on December 10. Subversion and controversy Rockstar، which by 2026 will have a dozen studios around the world and more than 4,700 employees، devoted more than eight years to building the latest GTA instalment. Active production only began after the release of Rockstar’s previous game، “Red Dead Redemption II”، in 2018. It was a rocky ride to release. Shaken by a series of leaks in 2022 and the online release of stolen gameplay videos، the studio postponed the launch twice، then suffered a new round of leaks last summer. The games have also regularly been accused of glorifying violence and illegal behaviour as GTA has carved out a place in pop culture as a symbol of subversion، unafraid to mock the flaws of American society. Players can run over pedestrians، sell drugs and shoot at the police. “It’s a series that is famous for being always over the top in terms of its representation of violence and different forms of abuse or harassment، for its representations of gender”، said Paolo Ruffino، a lecturer in digital cultures at King’s College London. “I don’t expect to see necessarily major controversies unless there is something completely new، ” he added. But as a consequence of its scandalous legacy، several countries have banned the saga. No official release is currently planned in Russia، China، Lebanon or Qatar. — AFP

53bf28c36494803d: The activist admits his mental state has been negatively affected by the 10-year sentence increase
Originally published on Global Voices
Joshua Wong released from Lai Chi Kok Reception Centre on June 17, 2019. HKFP's File photo.

This article was originally published by Hong Kong Free Press on November 16, 2026. The following version is edited and republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

In a letter from a Hong Kong prison earlier this year, jailed activist Joshua Wong expressed dread over the looming sentence in his foreign collusion case. “Fretting about whether it’s 2032 or 2037, my mental state is hardly all right,” he wrote in Chinese, weighing when he might regain his freedom.
The agony inevitably stems from this: What if it’s 2037? Well, it’s easy [for people] to sympathise in the moment, but it’s difficult to be consistent, and it will only get harder.

The 30-year-old pro-democracy activist has already spent almost six years behind bars over various offences and was set for release in January 2026, until authorities charged him last year with conspiring to collude with foreign forces — the second case against him under the Beijing-imposed national security law. His case is one of the most high-profile examples of changing judicial norms in Hong Kong.
A prison letter Joshua Wong wrote to friend and former fellow student activist Louis Lee in February 2026. This photo was taken on September 30, 2026. Photo by Kyle Lam/HKFP. Used with permission.

On November 5, just two months before he was due to be released, a court sentenced him to 10 more years in prison for colluding with foreign forces. He is now expected to serve until late 2036, when he turns 40.

Standing in the courtroom as his new sentence was announced, Wong shook his head slightly and made notes, but appeared calm. Judge William Tam ruled that Wong’s offence was one of a “grave nature” under the national security law, which carries a minimum penalty of 10 years in jail and up to life imprisonment.
The judge knocked off three years from a 13-year starting sentence for Wong’s guilty plea.

In prison correspondence shared with HKFP by two close friends ahead of Wong’s sentencing, the former poster child of Hong Kong’s democracy movement had at times reflected on the weight of facing an additional decade behind bars. He expressed anxiety over fading from the memory of his friends — and from society at large. In one letter, Wong wrote:
I have no idea how much more I will lose in the passing of time. Responsibility is, in fact, response-ability. But who will respond? I can’t help but ponder and doubt.

Once a pro-democracy activist dedicated first and foremost to Hong Kong’s political future, Wong began campaigning as a charismatic, eloquent student leader who dared to stand up to the authorities — even to Beijing. Hong Kong is an overseas territory of China, and has increasingly been pressured to conform to China’s political goals in recent years, despite agreements that Hong Kong would retain “a high degree of autonomy” when handed over to China in 1997. A Netflix documentary about him is succinctly titled “Joshua: Teenager vs. Superpower.”

Yet, after years behind bars, Wong has changed. The teenager who focused single-mindedly on Hong Kong’s democracy movement has become even more caring for those around him despite being separated by prison walls, according to his friends.
Tiffany Chin, a former student activist who campaigned alongside Wong, said. The pair were once romantically involved and are now friends. She shared:
For me, it doesn’t feel like we’re the only ones supporting him. In fact, he has been supporting people on the outside in his own way.
And, with the political causes he once championed now firmly crushed, Wong has turned inward to reflect on himself. In another letter, he wrote:
We had held such high aspirations for society from a young age, we should hold ourselves to the same standard. Only by refusing a life of mediocrity can we be worthy of the world we envisioned.
From “robot” to caring friend

On a bright summer day in June 2025, while serving a sentence for subversion at Stanley Prison, Wong was arrested behind bars and brought to court the same day on a fresh charge of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces.
The prosecution came without warning. That day, Chin and Louis Lee, another longtime friend of Wong’s, rushed to the court after hearing the news, but failed to see him in person.

Authorities accused him of conspiring with Nathan Law — another high-profile, pro-democracy student activist — in 2020 to collude with foreign elements, citing Wong’s sharing of Law’s social media posts calling for international sanctions against Hong Kong as evidence.
The unexpected new charge was devastating to Wong. That month, he confessed he was under a lot of pressure — a vulnerability he rarely showed in the past, Chin said.

After so many prison terms and all the ups and downs over the last decade… he seldom openly showed vulnerability. So when he felt the need to say so bluntly that he was not OK, I truly believed he wasn’t.

Having begun campaigning at the age of 14, Wong has been in and out of prison throughout his years of activism. He now has a total of eight criminal convictions, including three separate offences linked to unlawful assembly and two national security offences.
Joshua Wong is photographed inside the Lai Chi Kwok Reception Centre on March 4, 2021. Photo via HKFP. Used with permission.

Born in 1996 to a Christian family – one year before Hong Kong was handed over to China from British rule – Wong rose to prominence in 2011 when he co-founded student protest group Scholarism amid a public outcry against a proposed patriotic education curriculum.

The following year, Scholarism activists occupied the forecourt outside Hong Kong government headquarters and staged a hunger strike to protest what they described as a “brainwashing” curriculum. In a widely reported encounter, the teenager Wong twice refused to shake hands with then-city leader Leung Chun-ying, who visited the protest site alongside education officials.
Hundreds of thousands of people rallied behind Wong and his fellow student activists, forcing the government to back down and shelve the proposal.

But the teenage campaigner was also viewed as somewhat distant and domineering among the inner circle of Scholarism. Lee, who mainly handled protest logistics at that time, described his relationship with Wong as “almost like that of a boss and subordinate.”

Chin, who joined Scholarism around 2013, similarly described Wong as a deeply rational figure who seldom expressed his emotions. “Ten years ago, everyone described him as someone without many feelings,” she said. “Like a robot.”
Wong might even come across as “rude,” she added, noting that he rarely said thanks to others during that period.

A large part of Wong’s youth coincided with a period of escalating social movements in Hong Kong. Just two years after the anti-patriotic education protests, the city saw the 79-day Umbrella Movement in 2014. Wong, then aged 17, took centre stage in mobilising public support for student protesters, who demanded democratic reform and universal suffrage.

In a demonstration that sparked the Umbrella Movement, Wong and other student leaders led protesters into the forecourt of the government headquarters in an action dubbed “Reclaiming Civic Square,” seeking to escalate their campaign. That eventually resulted in Wong’s first criminal conviction.

In 2016, Wong and fellow student leaders Alex Chow and Nathan Law were found guilty of unlawful assembly. Though initially spared prison, Wong later served around 69 days behind bars – his first jail term – following a government appeal in 2017. His penalty was ultimately quashed by the Court of Final Appeal in 2018.

Scholarism disbanded in 2016. Wong and several former members, as well as young activists like Law, went on to establish Demosisto, a political party advocating for “democratic self-determination” in the city. Wong served as general secretary.
Lee and Chin did not join the new party, and they grew estranged from Wong during that period.

That year, Law was elected to the Legislative Council, making him the youngest lawmaker in Hong Kong history at the age of 23. He won over 50,000 votes, giving Demosisto a strong popular mandate. The prospect of youth democracy activism appeared bright at the time, but Law was eventually disqualified from his seat in 2017 following an oath-taking controversy.
From left: Joshua Wong, Agnes Chow, and Nathan Law, photographed on March 10, 2018. Photo via HKFP. Used with permission.
Reconnections
It was only after Wong’s detention in late 2020 that Lee and Chin reconnected with him, beginning with an exchange of letters.

In 2019, citywide protests and unrest triggered by a controversial extradition bill engulfed the city. Wong and Demosisto were heavily involved in the protests, with the activist frequently lobbying foreign governments to impose sanctions on Hong Kong officials and halt the export of crowd control equipment to the city’s police force.

Then, in June 2020, Beijing imposed the national security law, effectively crushing political dissent in the city. Demosisto disbanded on the eve of the law’s enactment, while Nathan Law left Hong Kong in self-exile.
Written by Hong Kong Free Press
7afe3ce88c6c477c: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — Retirement preparedness in Malaysia may have less to do with income levels and more to do with the financial habits, behaviours and support systems people develop throughout their lives, according to research by Universiti Sains Malaysia, commissioned by FWD Malaysia (FWD). While rising living costs remain a significant challenge for many households, the study found that factors such as financial literacy, long-term planning and social influence play a critical role in determining retirement readiness across both lower- and middle-income segments. The research also found that only 12.5 per cent of retirees surveyed had high levels of financial resources, highlighting the financial vulnerabilities many Malaysians face as they approach retirement. The findings challenge the common perception that retirement security is primarily determined by earnings. Instead, they suggest that the ability to make informed financial decisions, build positive financial habits and stay committed to long-term goals may be equally important in shaping financial outcomes later in life. For many Malaysians, however, long-term planning often takes a back seat to more immediate financial concerns. Rising household expenses, family commitments and economic uncertainty can make retirement feel like a distant priority. “Our research shows that retirement preparedness is ultimately a lifelong journey,” said Mak See Sen, chief executive officer of FWD Insurance Berhad. “Income is important, but what often makes the difference is whether people have the confidence, financial knowledge and support to make good decisions consistently over time. That’s why we believe financial literacy should start early, long before retirement becomes a concern.” The study also highlighted growing vulnerabilities among Malaysia’s middle-income population. Despite relatively stable earnings, many M40 households face competing financial demands, including housing commitments, children’s education expenses and the responsibility of supporting ageing parents. Among retirees surveyed, nearly 60 per cent reported living with one or more major physical illnesses such as heart disease, diabetes, arthritis or hypertension, underscoring the additional financial pressures associated with ageing. Often referred to as the “sandwich generation”, many working adults find themselves balancing multiple responsibilities while trying to build their own financial security. According to FWD, these challenges often stem from financial behaviours and decisions formed earlier in life. As a result, improving retirement outcomes requires intervention long before individuals reach their peak earning years. To address this, FWD has invested RM5 million in a long-term financial literacy ecosystem designed to support Malaysians from childhood through young adulthood. Through programmes aimed at primary school, secondary school and university students, the initiative has reached more than 12,000 participants nationwide, particularly youths from low-income and financially vulnerable backgrounds. These efforts include FWD’s long-standing collaboration with Junior Achievement (JA) Malaysia, which equips students with essential financial literacy and entrepreneurship skills through experiential learning programmes. In addition to its school and university-based initiatives, FWD also partners with Junior Achievement (JA) Malaysia to equip young Malaysians with practical financial literacy and entrepreneurship skills. Through this collaboration, students gain exposure to real-world financial concepts and hands-on learning experiences that help build confidence in managing their financial future. Research findings also point to the importance of social influence in shaping financial behaviour. Family members, friends, mentors and community networks often play a significant role in determining how people approach money and long-term planning. The study further found that approximately one-third of retirees exhibited signs of cognitive challenges including forgetfulness, reinforcing the importance of building financial confidence and resilience earlier in life. Recognising this, FWD has focused on community-based partnerships that encourage peer-to-peer learning and support. Through its collaboration with ARUS Academy under the Fun(d) for Life: University Edition programme, participants are encouraged to apply their learning and share it within their own communities. “As Malaysia moves towards an ageing society, we need to help people build resilience long before they encounter financial difficulties. Financial literacy is not just about understanding money. It is about creating the confidence and capability to make choices that lead to greater security, independence and peace of mind.” Mak adds. FWD believes insurers and takaful operators have an important role to play beyond providing protection products. By investing in education, community empowerment and financial confidence-building, organisations can contribute to stronger long-term financial outcomes for future generations of Malaysians.

088840b2862670e5: PUTRAJAYA, Nov 18 — The Court of Appeal today reserved its decision on businessman Tan Sri Tan Kok Ping’s appeal against a High Court ruling ordering him to pay RM350,000 in damages to Penang Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow for defamation. A three-member panel comprising Justices Datuk Azizul Azmi Adnan, Datuk Aliza Sulaiman and Datuk Seri Latifah Mohd Tahar reserved its decision after hearing submissions from Tan’s counsel, Datuk K. Kirubakaran, and Chow’s counsel, K. Simon Murali. On December 3, 2024, the Penang High Court ordered Tan to pay RM350,000 in damages after finding that remarks he made at a press conference on October 18, 2023, were defamatory. The remarks, made in Mandarin, were translated as “incompetent”, “ignorant” and “shameless”. High Court judge Datuk Quay Chew Soon found that the remarks, which were published by six Chinese-language newspapers and an English-language daily, had seriously damaged Chow’s reputation. In his submissions before the Court of Appeal today, Kirubakaran argued that the High Court judge had erred in law and fact in finding the three words defamatory. He said Chow had merely stated the Malay translations of the three words as their alleged defamatory meanings in his statement of claim. However, in his witness statement, Chow had expanded on the meanings, attributing to the remarks a more injurious defamatory meaning than that originally pleaded. Kirubakaran argued that Chow could not rely on a more defamatory meaning than the one set out in his statement of claim, as doing so would be prejudicial to Tan. He added that Chow should be bound by his pleadings. He further submitted that the High Court judge had erred in accepting Chow’s self-serving explanation of the impugned remarks. “There was an absence of evidence from members of the community or third parties or experts on Chinese language as to the meaning and effect of the impugned statement on Chow,” he said. In response, Simon Murali urged the Court of Appeal to dismiss Tan’s appeal, submitting that the High Court’s judgment was beyond reproach and contained no appealable errors. He further submitted that the High Court judge had correctly considered the relevant facts and applied the applicable legal principles in finding that Tan was motivated by malice in making the defamatory remarks. Simon Murali said there was no appealable error in the High Court judge’s finding that Tan’s defence of justification was unsustainable. He added that the High Court had also rightly rejected Tan’s defences of qualified privilege and fair comment. Chow filed the defamation suit against Tan, who is the life honorary president of the Penang Chinese Chamber of Commerce, in January 2024 over remarks made by Tan concerning the sale of state land in Batu Kawan. 03692ec60cac1bbf: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. In response, Wiltschko says that “human perception isn’t a workaround for AI”. “Language models learn from what people have written. Our model learns from what people smell. Smell is ultimately a human experience, so the model has to learn from humans to bridge chemistry and perception. That’s what lets it predict how people will experience a scent as well as the human nose does.”

Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”

In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.
For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”
This article has been updated with an additional comment from Alex Wiltschko.
b65e40315f75a8fe: PUTRAJAYA, Nov 18 — The Court of Appeal today increased an Arabic language teacher’s prison sentence from six to 10 years and ordered him to be caned twice for sexually assaulting an eight-year-old female pupil seven years ago. A three-member panel chaired by Datuk Mohamed Zaini Mazlan, together with Datuk Ahmad Shahrir Mohd Salleh and Datuk Dean Wayne Daly, unanimously allowed the prosecution’s cross-appeal to enhance the sentence imposed on Ahnaf Afiq Shairul Bazri, 35. “We set aside the sentence imposed by the High Court and substitute it with eight years’ imprisonment for the offence under Section 14(a) of the Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017, and a further two years’ imprisonment under Section 16(1) of the same Act, together with two strokes of the cane. “The court also orders the respondent to undergo counselling and police supervision for two years upon completion of his prison sentence,” said Justice Mohamed Zaini. The panel dismissed Ahnaf Afiq’s appeal against his conviction and sentence imposed by the Muar High Court on March 11, 2026. It further ordered that a warrant of committal be issued immediately for him to begin serving his sentence, while the bail money is to be refunded to his surety. In a brief judgment, Justice Mohamed Zaini said the court was not satisfied with the sentence imposed by the High Court, taking into account the gravity of the offences committed by the accused. “The victim was only eight years old, and the accused had abused his position and the trust placed in him as a teacher entrusted with the care and education of pupils. “These were significant aggravating factors. “The accused also admitted to taking the victim into the room and closing the door. “In the circumstances, we find that the conviction is safe and dismiss the appeal against conviction,” he said. He said the victim, who testified as the second prosecution witness (SP2), had given clear and detailed evidence, which was further supported by her prompt disclosure to her mother (SP1) on the day of the incident. “We do not consider the discrepancy concerning SP2’s position when SP4, the victim’s schoolmate, entered the room to be sufficiently material to undermine the credibility of her testimony,” he said. On March 19, 2025, the Muar Sessions Court acquitted and discharged Ahnaf Afiq of the charges at the close of the defence case. However, the Muar High Court subsequently allowed the prosecution’s appeal, set aside the acquittal, convicted the accused and imposed a sentence of four years’ imprisonment and two strokes of the cane for the offence under Section 14(a). The Court further imposed an additional sentence of two years’ imprisonment and two strokes of the cane for the offence under Section 16(1), to take effect consecutively upon completion of the sentence imposed under Section 14(a). Ahnaf Afiq was charged with sexually assaulting an eight-year-old girl in the workroom of the library at a primary school in Muar, between 10.20 am and 11.20 am on October 3, 2019. Deputy public prosecutor Mohamed Aznin Mohamed Ariff appeared for the prosecution, while the accused was represented by lawyers Mohd Radzi Yatiman and Nor Hafizah Abdullah. — Bernama

f782436b47c7ae83: RIYADH، Nov 18 — A powerful explosion rattled homes in Riyadh on Wednesday، AFP journalists and residents said، as Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis pressed their campaign of attacks against the kingdom. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis also said they intercepted two cruise missiles — the latest in weeks of strikes targeting military، civilian and oil infrastructure. Residents said Wednesday’s explosion came without warning، with no mobile-phone alert issued beforehand as is usually the case during aerial threats. “The explosion was extremely loud، ” said a resident in northern Riyadh. “Hearing a blast without receiving a warning is very frightening.” An AFP journalist said doors throughout her home swung open and the lights briefly went out. The location of the explosion was not immediately clear، but residents told AFP they saw smoke near Riyadh’s airport in the northeast of the city. In October، a deadly attack targeting Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 14 people and injured hundreds، forcing the suspension of flights for two weeks. Within minutes، the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile launched by the group towards the Riyadh region. Earlier، the coalition had reported intercepting another cruise missile also heading for the same region. Saudi civil defence authorities also said they had activated early warning systems in the southern regions of Jazan، Najran and Khamis Mushait، near the Yemeni border. The Saudi-led coalition، which backs neighbouring Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its war with the Houthis، has battled a surge in attacks since hostilities reignited in July. The long-running civil war in Yemen، one of the world’s poorest countries، had been largely dormant after a ceasefire went into effect in 2022. The Houthis are now nearing Aden، the government’s interim capital، having made sweeping territorial gains since the war resumed. Since the summer، more than 1,600 people have been killed and over 300,000 displaced by the fighting، according to the United Nations. — AFP

43c6c4ac0068ccff: JAKARTA، Nov 18 — Indonesia’s central bank has raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to six per cent، a pre-emptive move aimed at stabilising the weakening rupiah and containing inflation amid heightened global economic uncertainty. Bank Indonesia (BI) Communications Department executive director Ramdan Denny Prakoso said the decision was made at the central bank’s two-day Board of Governors meeting which concluded on Wednesday. The meeting also saw the Deposit Facility rate raised by 25 basis points to 5.25 per cent and the Lending Facility rate by the same margin to 6.75 per cent. “The increase is a measure to further strengthen rupiah exchange rate stabilisation against the impact of rising global uncertainty، as well as a pre-emptive measure to keep inflation in 2026 and 2027 within the target range of 2.5 per cent، plus or minus one percentage point، ” he said in a statement on Wednesday. The latest increase marks BI’s first benchmark rate hike since June 18، when it raised the rate to 5.75 per cent، a level maintained for the following four months through October. Ramdan said the rupiah stood at Rp18,245 (RM4.11) against the US dollar on Tuesday، weakening 0.66 per cent from its end-October level، amid persistent global uncertainty and weak foreign investor sentiment in the domestic stock market. He said the central bank would continue directing monetary policy towards strengthening rupiah exchange rate stability while maintaining accommodative macroprudential measures to support lending to the real sector and preserve financial system stability. He said BI would also optimise foreign exchange intervention through offshore non-deliverable forward transactions، as well as spot and domestic non-deliverable forward transactions in the domestic market، alongside measures to strengthen banking liquidity. “Going forward، BI projects that the rupiah exchange rate will remain stable، supported by its commitment، attractive yields، inflation controlled within the target، and favourable domestic economic prospects، ” he said. Ramdan said global financial market volatility remained elevated due to continuing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East، growing political instability in Europe and expectations of further monetary tightening in the United States. He said BI expected global economic growth to remain weak at around 3.1 per cent in 2026، with inflation remaining elevated at approximately 4.6 per cent، prompting investors to reduce portfolio investments in emerging markets. Despite external pressures، he noted that Indonesia’s economy expanded by 5.47 per cent year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026، accelerating from 5.29 per cent in the preceding quarter، supported mainly by domestic consumption and investment. He said BI projected Indonesia’s economy to grow between 4.9 and 5.7 per cent in 2026، while annual inflation eased to 3.23 per cent in October from 3.28 per cent in September، remaining within the central bank’s target range. On capital flows، Ramdan said foreign portfolio investment in Indonesia’s stock market recorded net outflows of US$900 million in the fourth quarter up to November 16، although overall capital flows registered net inflows of US$4.80 billion، supported by government global sukuk and bond issuances، as well as inflows into government securities. He said Indonesia’s foreign exchange reserves stood at US$146.8 billion at the end of October، equivalent to 5.3 months of imports، while bank lending grew 13.21 per cent year-on-year in the same month. To support financing، he said BI was preparing to introduce macroprudential liquidity incentives of up to three per cent of banks’ third-party funds from Dec 1، targeting lending to businesses that support job creation and micro، small and medium enterprises. The central bank also plans to introduce cross-currency repurchase transactions by March 2027، allowing banks to obtain rupiah liquidity using foreign currency-denominated BI securities and sukuk as collateral، he added. — Bernama
d1a7d532fe6d842b: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) is stepping up supervisory measures and regulatory requirements to ensure financial institutions remain resilient against evolving cyber threats, including their ability to detect, respond to and recover from cyber incidents, Governor Datuk Seri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said. He said financial institutions had also made significant investments to strengthen their cybersecurity defences following recent cyberattacks. “As far as BNM is concerned, we place very strong emphasis on cybersecurity. We strengthen their resilience through supervisory measures and the ongoing enhancement of our Risk Management in Technology (RMiT). “We also work closely with the National Cyber Security Agency (NACSA) and financial institutions to strengthen the sector’s cyber preparedness, resilience and operational readiness,” he said at a press conference on third-quarter gross domestic product performance today. Abdul Rasheed cautioned that as the country becomes increasingly digital and interconnected, financial institutions must be prepared for cyber incidents and even banking service disruptions, which could occur as part of everyday operations. He said cybersecurity was a shared responsibility involving regulators, financial institutions and consumers, urging the public to remain vigilant against scams, impersonation attempts and other cyber threats. He advised consumers to verify information received through social media, emails and other communication channels against trusted and official sources before sharing it or responding. He also highlighted BNM’s “3S” approach — Soal, Sekat, Sebar (Ask, Block, Share) — as a simple reminder for the public to protect themselves against cyber threats. — Bernama
a38995cedd88a3d8: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said has issued a statement calling on the relevant authorities to explain how the Federal Territories Pardons Board meeting minutes that discussed Datuk Seri Najib Razak’s conditional pardon had been made public. Speaking as Umno’s information chief, Azalina questioned if the minutes are officially declassified, when and by whom. The alleged copies of the meeting details are now being circulated on the internet, and first reported by news portal Malaysiakini. All documents related to the Pardons Board are official secrets, and there are processes to observe before it can be made public. Umno’s statement referred to the DAP’s Tony Pua as the source of the leaked minutes. “For documents with official secret status, the decision to declassify them must be made by the authority under Section 2C of the Official Secrets Act 1972 [Act 88] according to the applicable procedures,” said Azalina, who is also minister for law and institutional reforms. Malaysiakini said it had received the minutes from a well-placed source and alleged that the documents were declassified for court purposes, in response to the Bar Council’s legal challenge against the house arrest order. The documents do not appear to have been filed in court as of this morning, the portal noted. Umno said the “responsible parties” must provide an official explanation regarding its declassification status, if they have been declassified, when and by whom. Azalina also questioned the basis of authority and purpose of the purported declassification, and if circulating copies match the official record. “What is the basis of authority used, the procedure followed, and the purpose of the declassification? Does the declassification cover the entirety of the minutes, including related attachments, or only certain parts?” The minister asked. The alleged minutes detailed how FT Minister Hannah Yeoh and Attorney General Tan Sri Dusuki Mokhtar had opposed allowing Najib to serve the remaining jail sentence from his SRC International corruption conviction at home. Malaysiakini claimed Yeoh was also reluctant to sign off on the meeting. Najib is serving his prison sentence at home until August 2028 after he managed to pay the conditional RM50 million penalty.
12dd8e0a6a120bd3: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — The impact of the latest United States (US) restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres is still too early to assess, as developments surrounding the matter are still unfolding, said Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) Governor Datuk Seri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour. He said BNM concurred with the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry’s (Miti) stance that Malaysia would continue to engage with the relevant authorities on the matter. “This is one example where geo-economic risks are real and present, not just for us, but also for the rest of the world. “As far as Malaysia is concerned, as Miti has also stated, we will continue to uphold rules-based trade, remain open for business, and pursue our diversification strategy,” he said at the release of the third-quarter 2026 (3Q 2026) gross domestic product (GDP) data today. On Monday, the administration of US President Donald Trump issued a rule imposing new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres that enable Chinese companies to access advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips for training their AI models. The reports also stated that companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil would be required to obtain US export licences for the most advanced chips, as part of efforts to prevent their illegal diversion. Abdul Rasheed also emphasised that diversification remained a key strategy guiding Malaysia’s developments across various sectors, including date centres. He noted that of the 120 data centre companies operating in Malaysia, only 17, or about 13 per cent, were Chinese-owned, while the remainder originated from the US, Australia, Canada, and Malaysia. “This is where our investments (in data centres) are highly diversified. Therefore, the (US) restrictions are not expected to have a significant impact on data centre investments. “Based on our estimates of ongoing and planned projects, investment momentum in data centres is expected to remain strong at least until 2028,” he said, adding that sustained underlying demand for data centres would also create lasting economic linkages for Malaysia. According to Abdul Rasheed, the positive fundamentals are also consistent with the Malaysian Investment Development Authority’s (MIDA) approved information, communication and technology (ICT) investments, which increased to about RM38.9 billion in the first quarter of this year. **Impact of US midterm elections** Commenting on the US midterm election results, which could see the Democrats take control of Congress in January and increase scrutiny of the Trump administration’s tariff, data centre and AI policies, he said it was still too early to assess the potential implications for Malaysia’s economy as the situation continued to evolve. He stressed that strengthening the country’s economic fundamentals and foundations would help shield Malaysia from global developments and uncertainties. “On our part, we will continue to monitor the situation closely and assess its potential impact on the economy and financial markets, as well as the measures that we can put in place. “In addition, this is where buffers matter. That is why I always stress the importance of building up buffers during good times, when we are (in a) strong (position), so that we can always draw on them during difficult periods or in the event of unexpected developments,” he added. — Bernama
d9dd39f488a082d0: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — Proton’s Tanjong Malim plant rolled out over 23,000 vehicles last month. e2577fdfd894b330: HONG KONG, Nov 18 — Asian equities were mixed today as blockbuster earnings from Nvidia, which soothed concerns about the AI boom, were offset by concerns about a spy scandal that has engulfed the chip titan and shaken global markets. The tech sector — already hit by questions about profitability — has been strafed over the past week by claims that boss Jensen Huang had had a number of affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy who might have funnelled restricted chips to Beijing. The scandal forced Huang to step down on Thursday and has fanned worries about the chip titan, which is at the centre of a buildout that has helped propel world markets to record highs and boosted economic growth. In a highly anticipated earnings release Tuesday, the firm said third-quarter revenue topped expectations and doubled to more than $115 billion while net profit hit US$65.3 billion (RM269 billion). The firm also increased its forecast for next year’s revenue, predicting 75 percent growth, compared with a previous forecast of 70 percent. The figures suggested the artificial intelligence boom remained on track despite concerns that the vast sums pumped into the sector might not see returns any time soon, if at all. In a bid to reassure investors, interim CEO Colette Kress said it was “business as usual” at the firm, even after the loss of Huang, a pivotal player in the eye-watering explosion in the AI industry. The news sent Nvidia’s shares surging nearly five percent in after-hours US trade, while Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom were also sharply higher. Asian markets diverged as investors weighed the earnings with concerns about the scandal. Adding to the nervousness was news that the United States moved to tighten restrictions on Chinese access to chips, while Huang has agreed to meet US lawmakers on December 1 to answer questions about chips and national security concerns. Seoul ended the day up two percent as chip giants SK hynix and Samsung enjoyed big gains, though they are still well down for the week. Tokyo also advanced, with Advantest and tech investment giant SoftBank leading the way, while Taipei was lifted by an uptick in TSMC. Shanghai, Bangkok and Jakarta also rose. However, Hong Kong, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Manila and Mumbai all fell. There are “still lots of unknowns for the stock that create the overhangs that investors are worried about. But the earnings show it’s still in very good shape”, wrote Neil Wilson at Saxo Markets. And SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes added: “The investigations and allegations aren’t findings of wrongdoing, but they certainly aren’t the backdrop Nvidia would have chosen for its earnings presentation. “Interim CEO Colette Kress now has to manage the commercial business while the company’s founder remains the subject of an extraordinary political and corporate struggle. “The broader institutional positioning suggests why even an outstanding earnings forecast may struggle to generate the kind of rally investors once took for granted.” Also in focus this week is the planned New York debut Thursday of AI giant Anthropic following an initial public offering that is expected to value the firm at as much as US$1.4 trillion. While Anthropic is widely seen as the leader for AI products, Nvidia has been dubbed the “central bank” of the industry for its investments in startups and providing backstops on loans. By the end of the week, traders are hoping to have more certainty about the commercial future of a technology that has been long on hype but short on profitable products. Oil prices continued to fall following reports that the world will swing to a surplus despite the US-Iran war. However, the commodity was supported by ongoing attacks in the Gulf region. Kuwait said today it was countering “hostile drone attacks”, with Washington’s allies on alert following a US strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. — AFP

e7bb5cbcc3bc3bfa: <!--kg-card-end: html--> A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion.

Gallup’s study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries.

A lot of the topline results won’t surprise anyone living in today’s constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling.

Young people in the United States, Canada, and UK reported the least interest in AI overall, with only 20% saying they used it once a day or more. Almost 40 percent of young people in Brazil use it daily. Japan and Italy both come in around 35%. “Nearly half of young people in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada have used AI no more than a few times in the past month, including those who have not used it at all,” the researchers wrote.

Most of the respondents (82%) said they’d used AI to look up information, 68% asked it for advice, and 33% used it as a companion. Young people with online-only friends were more likely to use AI for companionship, “although these patterns do not establish whether AI companionship supplements or substitutes for human relationships,” they wrote.

The researchers discovered that people in different countries felt wildly different about their AI buddies. Almost half of Australians with AI friends rated the relationship as “high quality” and only 12% of young people in Poland did. Mostly, though, people thought of their AI friends as mid: “In most countries [...] young people are more likely to give their AI companionship a medium rating than either a high or low rating.”

People who used AI as a friend also reported higher levels of loneliness, the study found. “However, the findings cannot determine whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely, whether AI companionship influences their social experiences or whether other circumstances help explain these relationships,” the researchers wrote.

The researchers also asked young people what they do online all day and the overwhelming majority (72%) said they spend their time scrolling short form content, mostly TikTok and Instagram. It’s also how they deal with loneliness, with six in 10 young people participating in this study reporting that they often or always scroll through online content when lonely.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> They also said scrolling works to dispel loneliness almost equally as well as hanging out with a friend in real life: “Although scrolling is more commonly used when young people feel lonely, those who use scrolling or in-person time as coping strategies report nearly identical levels of perceived helpfulness.”

Still, people who reported strong in-person friendships said they felt lonely less often, while online friendships have the same effect on loneliness regardless of how participants ranked the quality of those friendships. “No comparable difference appears across levels of online-only friendship quality,” the authors wrote. Having in-person relationships seemed to be what mattered most: “Higher loneliness is also more common among young people who frequently communicate online with strangers or online-only friends than among those who frequently communicate with in-person friends or family members.”

The relationships between loneliness, online friendships, and AI is complex and a person’s material conditions shape how they form friendships more than their access to a chatbot or how they use social media. The researchers’ analysis of young people who said they have no trusted adults in their lives makes that clear.

“Further analysis identifies several characteristics associated with having none of these friendship modes, but one stands out in particular: not having a trusted adult outside the family,” the researchers wrote. “This association remains substantial after accounting for country or residence, gender, age, urbanicity, and parent/ caregiver relationship quality.”

The study’s authors warned about reading too much into these results. “These assessments should be compared cautiously with those for human friendships examined in this report, as young people may have different expectations of what makes an AI companion or human friendship meaningful or supportive,” they wrote. In general, people don’t have the same expectations of a chatbot that they do someone they know in real life.

“The broader message is not that one form of connection is inherently better or worse, but that the quality of young people’s relationships and the wider social context in which they exist matter greatly,” the study concluded.

461a1fe87414da12: A teacher who believes a student’s term paper may have been written by a large language model (LLM) can use a tool for detecting artificial intelligence-generated text to help confirm their suspicions. But the teacher may want to think twice before putting all their trust in the detector.  Researchers from MIT and Cornell University showed that such detection tools, which are AI models themselves, can be fooled by AI-generated text disguised to appear as if it were written by a human. Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs. In a new paper, the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes. They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch. In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy. This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. It could also be used by cybersecurity experts to prevent email phishing scams or identify search engine optimization fraud. “There are many high-stakes contexts where people really care about the identity of the author, from scientific publishing to short story competitions. We’ve shown that test-time adaptation allows your AI detector to be much more robust, even with continual adversarial behavior by AI users,” says study co-author Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who also holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). He is joined on the paper by lead author Kevin Ren, graduate student at Cornell Tech, and senior author Nikhil Garg, an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Duping the detectors The proliferation of LLMs that generate human-like text has led to a plethora of commercial AI-detection tools to help people identify whether a piece of writing was authored by a human. But these detection tools can fail when the text they evaluate significantly differs from the text they were taught to identify. This is known as a distribution shift. Detector developers typically train their models by gathering text from the internet that they know to be either AI- or human-generated. They train the model to tell the difference.  However, once the detector is released, people might change the way they write or the way they use AI to generate text.  For instance, a human in 2030 may write about different topics using new analogies that weren’t common for someone writing in 2010. A detector trained with 2010 data might be unfamiliar with this new writing style and incorrectly mark human-written text as AI-generated. The release of a detection model also creates a cat-and-mouse game between its developers and users who want to bypass it. These individuals can run AI-generated text through an automated “humanizer” software tool that modifies it to appear human-written to the detector. “After the company releases a model, a bunch of ‘humanizers’ pop up to try to beat it, so the company tries to incorporate this humanized text into their training so the detector can identify it, and so on. It’s like rinse-and-repeat. The cycle can go on forever,” says Ren. The researchers explored whether test-time adaptation (TTA) can make an AI detector resilient to these distribution shifts. Adaptation in action In TTA, instead of freezing the model so it can’t change during deployment, researchers allow that model to adapt itself to incoming data after it has been released. For an AI text detector, these data are new pieces of text uploaded by users.  These data are unlabeled, so the detector developers don’t know which data were written by humans versus AI models. But these new data represent contemporary human and AI writing — exactly what the developers want the model to be able to predict.  With enough examples, the detector learns to identify patterns to determine which data are AI-generated and which are human-generated. The researchers studied TTA by creating datasets to contain a certain amount of AI-generated and human-generated text, but they don’t provide those labels to the model. They also used LLMs to generate some examples that resemble text written by AI to specifically evade a detector.  Then they performed the TTA training process and tested the model on ground-truth data. In experiments designed to mimic the natural shift in human language over time, a detector that used TTA was 85 percent accurate, while traditional methods only achieved 73 percent accuracy. And when it came to writing designed to thwart detection tools, existing methods could only identify about 27 percent, while TTA enabled the model to catch more than 93 percent of disguised text. “TTA has the potential to really help deployed AI-detection models in terms of being able to proactively address this iterative ‘gaming’ behavior by adversarial AI users,” Ren says. Adapting to shifts in human writing behavior is a more difficult TTA problem, since the shifts are slower and occur in more subtle ways, he adds. The researchers caution that TTA may not always be an effective solution as future LLMs produce more natural-sounding language and it becomes harder to find verifiable human text to use for training. “It isn’t entirely clear if this will be a solvable problem,” Raghavan says. “There are some big, open questions about how you should think about science, writing, and art in a world where it is infeasible to tell the difference between human-generated content and AI content.” In the future, the researchers want to explore similar strategic domains where TTA could be useful and build better benchmarking tools to help engineers improve these AI detection models in a dynamic fashion. This project used API credits provided by Pangram to use their AI text detectors.
