7a58b0e7934fec5c: US president Donald Trump and his cronies are eager to normalise relations with Russia in exchange for lucrative oil deals. In doing so, they are advancing Russian president Vladimir Putin’s strategy of systematically isolating Ukraine by making its defense so costly that popular support for the country in Europe evaporates.
After more than four years of full-scale war, it is abundantly clear that Russia cannot win on the battlefield. Nor can it force Ukraine to surrender through economic or political means.

The Kremlin’s next step was to secure Trump’s assistance. Putin’s goal at the August 2025 summit in Anchorage, Alaska—as evidenced by statements from multiple Russian officials—was to persuade the Trump administration to pressure Ukraine to surrender.
When the Ukrainian government stood up to American pressure, the Kremlin concluded that it needed the Trump administration’s active involvement on Russia’s behalf.

The ongoing discussions about a return of US companies to Russia, led by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Trump’s special envoy (and fellow New York real-estate baron) Steve Witkoff, reflect that effort.

Using nebulous promises of fossil-fuel profits “after the end of the war” as a carrot, Putin is seeking to align Trump’s pecuniary interests with Russia’s strategic objectives, giving Trump a reason to declare the war over or, better yet, to force Ukraine to capitulate.
Never mind the years of horrific conflict, untold war crimes, millions of people killed or displaced, and the generational trauma; Trump wants his cut.

What is baffling is that this bribe will not benefit the US, individual American companies, or business executives. It may briefly enrich those in Trump’s orbit, but profits are unlikely to last in a country where murder and expropriation are a material business risk.

The cynical expression “maski-show” (borrowed from a 1990s TV show) and the more straightforward term “raiding” describe schemes in which masked, armed individuals storm companies’ headquarters, forge documents, or force ostensibly legal changes in ownership and corporate structure.
The Trump administration and some American executives fail to understand that, for the Kremlin, agreements and business deals are not opportunities for mutually beneficial cooperation.
They are tools the Russian elite uses to hold the other side to its commitments while discarding its own obligations as soon as doing so becomes profitable.

It is difficult to convey to a Western audience just how corrupt Russian politicians and functionaries are. Russia’s Byzantine system of overlapping criminal schemes has no real equivalent in the West.

Yet American investors and businesses have repeatedly fallen victim to these practices. Bill Browder and George Soros lost billions of dollars when their Russian assets were taken. Paul Klebnikov, the editor of Forbes Russia, was murdered outside his office in 2004.

Oil executive Bob Dudley was driven out of the country. And Paul Whelan, a corporate security executive, was jailed in 2018 and spent almost six years in prison before a prisoner swap allowed him to return to the US.

Many Western and East Asian firms operating in Russia have also been forced to sell their assets for token prices. Others have been unable to repatriate their profits or have been forced to surrender control of their operations.
Carlsberg and Danone were forced to sell their Russian assets at below-market value, and ExxonMobil recorded a US$4.6 billion write-down in 2022 after announcing its withdrawal from Russia.
The Kremlin later transferred its stake in the Sakhalin-I oil field to a Rosneft subsidiary, though ExxonMobil has since signed a preliminary agreement aimed at recovering its losses.
Many other companies—including Ford, Nissan, Mazda, Hyundai, Shell, Société Générale, and TotalEnergies—have suffered enormous losses.

Far from being an El Dorado of the East, Russia is a country of approximately 143 million people with degraded infrastructure and a stagnant economy propped up by unsustainable government defense spending.

Given low incomes, it is hardly a lucrative market, and local oligarchs or members of the security services can and do “relieve” owners of profitable assets. This has happened many times already, most notably with the Sakhalin-I and Sakhalin-II oil projects.

Yet the apparent quid pro quo is clear. In exchange for access to Russian oil and gas, the Kremlin wants an end to US sanctions, which it hopes will enable it to continue its war against Ukraine and Europe indefinitely.
If Russia succeeds in bribing the right US officials to take its side, the focus will switch to Europe, which will then come under pressure to abandon Ukraine.
US officials participating in such transactions would likely become international pariahs, potentially making them even more dependent on Russia. The Kremlin cultivates such relationships.

Former German chancellor Gerhard Schröder and Karin Kneissl, Austria’s former pro-Russia foreign minister, both accepted sinecures at Russian energy companies after leaving political office. They soon found themselves welcome in Moscow and reviled everywhere else.

Putin’s maniacal obsession with destroying Ukrainian sovereignty and erasing Ukrainian identity will not stop. But Ukraine has demonstrated its determination to keep fighting, with national polls showing that Ukrainians overwhelmingly reject surrender. Unable to break Ukraine, Putin will turn his aggression against Europe.

The Kremlin has already sharply increased its hostile activity across Europe, targeting strategic defense infrastructure in Estonia and the Czech Republic, attempting to bring down civilian cargo planes bound for North America, threatening high-ranking government officials, and plotting assassinations of business leaders. European security agencies and leaders are warning of significant Russian escalation within “months, not years”.

Trump’s betrayal of Ukraine will leave Europe to face Russia’s aggression alone, with the US potentially on the other side. And even if it fails, an attack on Europe will give Putin additional leverage to demand concessions and an opportunity to shift the domestic conversation away from his humiliating military defeat.
Andrew Kosenko is associate professor of economics at the School of Management at Marist College.

31272cf29b5ea3b6: From Moaz Nair

Four years after the 2022 general election, Malaysia finds itself on a promising economic trajectory. Investments are flowing in, new industries are taking root, and national development frameworks are beginning to show results.
Yet, beneath these encouraging macroeconomic headlines lies a quiet crisis that demands urgent, undivided attention from our elected leaders: the future of our university graduates.

Every year, tens of thousands of young Malaysians walk across convocation stages with hard-earned degrees, only to enter a job market that cannot absorb their qualifications. According to the statistics department and analyses by The Edge Malaysia, a staggering 35.2% of employed Malaysians with tertiary education are working in low- or semi-skilled jobs.

Over a third of our tertiary graduates are trapped in skill-related underemployment - driving e-hailing vehicles, working retail counters, or taking administrative roles that do not require a university education.

At a time when young Malaysians need bold economic stewardship, politicians must resist the perennial temptation of endless politicking and power struggles. Ensuring that our rising wave of graduates secures meaningful, high-income employment is not merely an educational challenge; it is the defining test of national governance.
Above all else, Malaysia must remain fiercely competitive in attracting quality foreign direct investment to generate high-income jobs.

Global capital is pragmatic and unforgiving. Multinational corporations pouring billions into artificial intelligence data centres, advanced manufacturing, and green technology require two things before they commit: unwavering political stability, and an immediately deployable, skilled local talent pool.
If political infighting threatens policy continuity, investors will seamlessly pivot to neighbouring markets. Maintaining stability is the bedrock upon which all job creation rests.
Structural reforms
However, attracting investment is only half the equation; preparing our youth to fill those roles requires sweeping structural reforms across ministries and campuses.

First, lawmakers and regulators must cut the bureaucratic red tape slowing down higher education. Education observers have long pointed out that sluggish certification processes under the Malaysian Qualifications Agency (MQA) leave university syllabuses trailing behind rapid technological shifts. In fast-moving fields like artificial intelligence and data science, a four-year curriculum approval cycle renders a degree obsolete before the first cohort even graduates. Streamlining MQA approvals is essential so universities can adapt in real time.

Second, ministries must break out of their silos. Under the Malaysia Higher Education Plan 2026-2035, the higher education ministry must work in lockstep with the economy ministry and the human resources ministry. Producing graduates without mapping them to actual industry demand is a recipe for wasted potential. Inter-ministerial coordination must align university intake numbers with real-world labour market needs.

Third, we must dismantle the lingering stigma against technical and vocational education and training (TVET). The numbers speak for themselves: TVET graduates currently boast an impressive 95.1% employment rate.

Supported by Malaysian Investment Development Authority tax incentives that have already greenlit roughly RM6 billion in private training investments, expanding TVET pathways offers a proven, direct pipeline into high-demand technical careers.

Fourth, our universities must be empowered as true engines of innovation through meritocracy. As international economists such as Harvard’s Dwight H Perkins have warned, reducing political interference in university leadership and prioritising strict merit in faculty hiring are critical to strengthening research and development. Without world-class research ecosystems and merit-based advancement, Malaysia will continue to lose its brightest minds to brain drain.

While government policy sets the stage, universities and students must also adapt to a shifting landscape. Relying solely on a generalist degree is no longer enough to guarantee a career. Institutions and undergraduates alike should pivot towards high-growth sectors - such as cybersecurity, healthcare, finance, and advanced engineering - while pairing academic theory with structured internships, industry micro-credentials, and professional certifications.

At the same time, as emphasised by Akademi Kenegaraan Malaysia, graduates must cultivate distinctly human competencies: adaptability, critical thinking, and strong communication skills that artificial intelligence cannot replicate.
Conclusion

Malaysia has worked hard since 2022 to regain its economic footing. Let us not squander this momentum on political distractions. Our politicians owe the next generation more than rhetoric - they owe them a stable, competitive economy where a Malaysian degree is a passport to prosperity, not a ticket to underemployment.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

A Malaysian applying for a licence, renewing a permit, or seeking government assistance should not have to navigate several websites, remember multiple passwords, or repeatedly submit the same information. Yet for some, accessing public services can still feel more complicated than it should.
We have become good at introducing digital platforms. The more important question is whether these platforms are making life easier for the rakyat.

Malaysia's digital transformation has brought improvements to public administration. Online apps, electronic payments, and digital records have reduced the need for physical visits and made many services more convenient.
These achievements deserve recognition. However, digital progress should not be measured simply by the number of apps launched or systems developed.
A government service is only successful when people can use it easily, reliably, and without unnecessary frustration.

Consider a small business owner applying for an operating licence. The application may be available online, but if the process still requires repeated document submissions, unclear approvals, or visits to different departments, digitalisation has merely changed the location of the bureaucracy.
The same applies to a parent seeking educational assistance, or an elderly person accessing healthcare services.
For these Malaysians, convenience matters more than the technology behind the system.

The 13th Malaysia Plan (2026-2030) places digital transformation and public service efficiency among Malaysia's development priorities. The challenge is ensuring that these ambitions translate into improvements that citizens can experience.

One persistent concern is fragmentation. Different agencies may operate separate systems with different registration requirements, procedures and user interfaces. While each platform may serve an administrative purpose, the combined experience can become confusing.
Citizens should not have to understand the organisational structure of government simply to obtain a service.

A more effective approach would focus on integrating services around people's needs. For example, starting a small business involves several administrative requirements. Instead of expecting entrepreneurs to navigate multiple agencies independently, government systems should provide clearer guidance and better coordination.
Similarly, families applying for assistance should not repeatedly provide information already held by public institutions, subject to appropriate privacy safeguards.

Another challenge is digital inclusion. Not every Malaysian has reliable internet access, the latest smartphone, or sufficient digital literacy to navigate complicated applications. Older citizens, rural communities, and people with disabilities may face additional difficulties.
Digital transformation should, therefore, preserve accessible alternatives while improving online services.

Three priorities deserve attention. First, government agencies should evaluate digital platforms through citizen experience rather than technological output. Processing times, successful applications, accessibility, and complaint resolution should become central performance indicators.

Second, greater emphasis should be placed on interoperability and administrative simplification. Agencies must improve information-sharing and eliminate unnecessary procedures before transferring them online.

Third, public servants should receive continuous training to provide responsive assistance across both digital and physical service channels. Technology cannot compensate for unclear procedures, weak coordination, or poor communication.

Importantly, public feedback must play a stronger role in evaluating service quality. When citizens report difficulties, their experiences should inform system improvements rather than disappear into administrative complaint channels.

Malaysia does not necessarily need another app whenever a service problem emerges. Sometimes, improving an existing platform, simplifying a form, or ensuring that someone answers a telephone call would make a greater difference. The objective should never be digitalisation for its own sake.

Malaysia's ambition to become a competitive digital economy depends partly on building public institutions that are efficient, trustworthy and responsive. A well-designed digital government should save citizens time, reduce costs, and make essential services easier to access.

The rakyat do not judge government efficiency by how many digital platforms exist. They judge it by whether applications are processed promptly, information is clear, and problems are resolved without unnecessary obstacles.
Malaysia's next public sector breakthrough may not require another digital platform. It may simply require making the services we already have work better for everyone.

Abd Rahim Romle is an associate professor and deputy dean at the Ghazali Shafie Graduate School of Government at Universiti Utara Malaysia. Ainur Rabiyatul Abd Rahim is a Master of Teaching English as a Second Language candidate at Universiti Putra Malaysia.

Spencer GreenOne of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast. While that remains the norm, Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared. I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays. I find turkeys fascinating, because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard. And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump. Receding since the late 1990s Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a big business. More than US$5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed. However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds (8 kilograms) of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds (6 kg). While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway. Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline. It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds (31 kg) in 1995 to 104 pounds (47 kg) in 2025. In other words, we’re eating almost eight times more chicken than turkey. Well, at least the 95% of Americans who aren’t vegetarian or vegan are. More costly at every step in the supply chain Government agencies, researchers and some pundits have identified two possible explanations for why Americans are eating less turkey. First: pocketbook concerns. Turkey often costs more than chicken, except when it goes on sale just before Thanksgiving. Over the past 25 years, wholesale turkey prices per pound averaged about 10% higher than chicken, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. That price, which is what big retailers typically pay, affects what you owe at checkout. For example, just before the 2026 Thanksgiving sales began, a Bell & Evans fresh whole turkey was going for $4.99 a pound, while a Bell & Evans fresh whole chicken cost $3.49 a pound at my local supermarket. That’s $1.50 a pound difference, which is significant in an economy where many people feel economically pinched. Nationally, you will see similar price differences, with fresh turkey being more expensive than fresh chicken. So, why is turkey pricier than chicken? Both turkeys and chickens are fed a diet of corn and soybeans. However, turkeys consume a higher percentage of soybeans. And soybeans currently cost about twice as much as corn. The latest data shows turkey feed costs are up almost 80%, without accounting for inflation, since 2000, while chicken feed costs have climbed only 60%. Too big for more families The second reason has to do with the size of today’s families. The typical Bell & Evans whole chicken my grocery store sells weighs approximately 4 pounds, while its fresh turkeys tend to range between 10 and 12 pounds. Big birds are handy if you have a lot of mouths to feed, but American families have shrunk over time. Today the average household includes only 2.5 people. The extra half-person does not represent children who are picky eaters or people who don’t like eating meat. It just means the typical family has between two and three people. That means cooking a 10-pound turkey results in 4 pounds of food per person, which is far more than almost anyone who is not a competitive food eater can consume. Cooking a 4-pound chicken, however, results in a more manageable 1.2 pounds of poultry per eater after getting rid of the bones, which make up about a quarter of a chicken. In simple terms, buying a whole chicken often results in one or two meals per person. Cooking a whole turkey often yields enough meat to produce meals for an entire week. Raymond Baker carves a turkey in 1948 while his wife and 16 kids surround him. Getty Images There are two more factors to consider. First, a 10-pound turkey costs a lot more than a 4-pound chicken. A 10-pound fresh bird at $4.99 a pound sets you back almost $50, while a $3.49-per-pound chicken that weighs 4 pounds costs under $14. Last, bigger birds take longer to roast. Cooking a 10-pound turkey in an oven takes about three hours, while a 4-pound chicken takes about two. That extra hour is a big burden in an increasingly time-pressed society. In case you were wondering, the world record for eating a turkey is held by Joey Chestnut. He gobbled down 9.35 pounds of turkey off the bone in 10 minutes in 2014. Please do not try that at home. What about wild turkeys? If you need to save money on turkey this holiday season, you should consider buying a frozen one. They are much cheaper. But can you save even more by going turkey hunting? Given all the large wild turkeys roosting in my backyard, I looked into what it would take. I live in Massachusetts, where hunting wild turkeys before Thanksgiving is legal. For much of the fall, hunters are allowed to use only bows and arrows. Beyond needing to be a proficient archer, they also have to purchase a sporting license, a turkey permit and an archery stamp for $95 each year. Having learned about that, I’m sticking to buying my turkeys in the supermarket. Jay L. 3411c497853951d7: From Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri
There is something more dangerous in politics than losing an election: winning one without understanding why.
The Melaka state election should be a wake-up call for both Pakatan Harapan (PH) and the Barisan Nasional-Perikatan Nasional (BN-PN) alliance.
BN-PN may celebrate its overwhelming victory, while PH may console itself with retaining a loyal support base. But beneath the celebrations and disappointments lies an uncomfortable reality.

PH has yet to demonstrate that it can significantly expand its appeal among Malay voters. BN-PN, meanwhile, has yet to prove that Malay political consolidation can translate into broader national acceptance.
Let the numbers speak.
In 2021, PH secured 114,457 votes, representing nearly 35.8% of the popular vote. In 2026, its tally increased to 143,273, but its vote share declined to 29.3%.
PH gained almost 29,000 votes, yet lost 6.5 percentage points of electoral support.
That is not an insignificant distinction.
PH is not necessarily losing its existing voters. It is losing the race to win over new ones.
More embarrassingly, all four seats won by PH went to DAP. PKR and Amanah failed to secure even a single constituency.

This raises an uncomfortable question: how can a coalition led by a Malay prime minister, supported by Malay ministers and commanding federal power, struggle so badly to translate that leadership into electoral success in Malay-majority constituencies?
PKR must ask whether its reformist identity still inspires confidence beyond its traditional supporters.
Amanah must explain why its supposedly progressive Islamic alternative has struggled to establish meaningful electoral traction.
A political party cannot survive indefinitely by reminding voters of what it once fought for. Eventually, voters want to know what it has delivered.
Reformasi cannot remain a historical slogan. It must become a measurable improvement in people's lives.
DAP should not celebrate too comfortably either.
Preliminary turnout estimates suggest that nearly 78% of Malay voters participated, compared with 59% of Chinese voters and 58% of Indian voters.
Although Chinese support for PH among those who voted appears relatively resilient, the weaker participation should worry DAP.
Chinese voters are not PH's permanent electoral fixed deposit.
They have expectations concerning education, economic opportunities, institutional reform and fair governance.
Fear of PAS may motivate some voters. But fear is not a substitute for trust, and disappointment can be expressed through silence at the ballot box.
Now consider BN-PN.
In 2021, BN and PN collectively received 200,472 votes while contesting separately. In 2026, their combined tally reached 308,668.
That represents an impressive 54% increase in absolute votes.
However, their combined popular vote share moved only marginally, from nearly 62.7% to 63.1%.
The alliance achieved a landslide in seats without achieving a comparable breakthrough in its combined share of the electorate.
This is not to diminish its victory. It is to distinguish electoral consolidation from a genuine expansion of political appeal.
And here lies BN-PN's greatest contradiction.

If its political identity increasingly revolves around Malay nationalism and religious conservatism, how does it intend to persuade Chinese, Indian, Sabah and Sarawak voters that their interests will be equally protected?
MCA and MIC may have won constituencies, but isolated victories do not automatically demonstrate a nationwide recovery of non-Malay confidence.
If Umno's ambition is merely to become more Malay than PAS, what exactly is MCA's future role? A political partner or a decorative guest at victory celebrations?
Defending Malay interests should never require making other communities feel politically expendable.
Malaysia's future cannot be secured by making one community believe that another community's progress represents its own defeat.
So what should PH do?
First, abandon the assumption that government performance automatically produces electoral loyalty.
I would propose an independent, constituency-level voter confidence audit, particularly among rural Malays, younger voters and the lower-middle-income population.
Ask those who rejected PH one simple question: what would convince you to reconsider?
Then publish measurable commitments on wages, housing, employment and living costs, with progress assessed every six months.

Second, PH must rebuild its political language. Ordinary Malaysians do not wake up thinking about coalition arithmetic. They wake up worrying about groceries, school expenses, wages and their children's future.
Third, stop treating criticism as hostility. Sometimes the harshest critics are identifying problems that loyal supporters refuse to acknowledge.
BN-PN should undertake an equally uncomfortable exercise: test its policies and political messaging among voters who do not share its ethnic or religious identity.

If the alliance cannot convince a substantial number of non-Malays that they have a secure future under its leadership, it risks becoming a powerful regional force with a national credibility problem.
The elections in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka offer valuable lessons, but they are not a reliable national forecast.
Umno should remember what happened after its victories in Melaka in 2021 and Johor in 2022.
Confidence turned into pressure for an early general election. Yet GE15 delivered BN its worst parliamentary performance up to that point.
Winning several states does not mean the keys to Putrajaya are already in your pocket.
Malaysia's electoral landscape is shaped by different demographics, local personalities, regional identities and economic expectations.
There is another reality politicians rarely admit openly: patronage, financial assistance and personal obligations remain influential in electoral politics.
Malaysians understand the saying, "orang berbudi kita berbahasa" ... kindness deserves appreciation.
But gratitude should never become political indebtedness.
A RM100 handout may ease household expenses today. A poor government can impose economic costs on an entire generation.

Ultimately, PH must learn to attract new voters rather than merely retain old supporters. BN-PN must learn to build confidence across communities rather than simply consolidate Malay political strength.
Neither side can claim to have solved Malaysia's political future.
An election determines who governs for five years. But the consequences of choosing the wrong leaders may be inherited for five generations.
Perhaps that is the greatest tragedy of Malaysian politics — our politicians are obsessed with counting the seats needed to capture power.
The people should be counting the price their children may eventually pay for it.
Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri is an analyst with Global Asia Consulting.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
428730d65d2647f0: On November 14, Asia fired up its wind machines and pyrotechnics for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, aka Eurovision Asia. Eleven countries competed – from Bangladesh and Bhutan to Vietnam and host country Thailand. Notably absent this first year were most of the continent’s most populous nations: China, India, Japan, Pakistan and Indonesia. The format was familiar: three-minute songs performed with no more than six people permitted on stage. But there was a distinct regional inflection in the staging, costuming and language choices. Regional flavour Many of the artists wove in elements of traditional sound and traditional dress, and artists expressed gratitude to the audience with the traditional Thai gesture wai (hands together). While the original Eurovision is hosted in a combination of English and French, Eurovision Asia was delivered in English only. But most artists performed either in their own language (36%) or a combination of that language with English (54%). Only South Korea’s song was performed entirely in English. By comparison, Eurovision 2026 featured 43% of songs entirely in English, 38% in languages other than English, and 19% multilingual. Musically, it was a diverse offering. The delicate lotus leaves of Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên and her back-up dancers broke into a high-energy opening number, Em Tiên. Malaysia’s Aina Abdul finished the show with a pitch-perfect power ballad, Bluest Sky. In between, audiences were treated to Cambodian and Bhutanese ballads, Bengali a capella, South Korean K-pop and, perhaps most surprisingly, Nepali rock. Girls to the front But it was the Philippines’ Carmelle – the youngest contestant, at 19 – who won the night with Sobra-Sobra. The focus of the empowering pop song in English and Tagalog was about Filipino women’s right to be who they want to be. “It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are. It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas,” Carmelle told The Guardian. Carmelle received 211 points, winning both the jury and the public vote, encompassing viewers from 183 countries and territories. With her victory, the Philippines has won the right to host Eurovision Asia in 2027. In the meantime, Carmelle will also perform at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria. Carmelle rehearsing Sobra-Sobra at the Eurovision Song Contest Asia. Eurovision Song Contest Asia Spectacle and snags Eurovision is known for its spectacle, and Eurovision Asia delivered, albeit on a more modest budget. Stage production made the most of stunning visual projections, smoke and flares. Eurovision is also known for its non-political stance, with political or ideological messages prohibited. But it has been more forgiving toward humanitarian statements. And at Eurovision Asia, Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai used the end of his set to call for support for his country as it recovers from the August flood disaster. The show was not without its hitches. Laos’ representative, Thinla, couldn’t hear her music due to an issue with her earpiece, so footage of her technical rehearsal was shown at the end of the performances to ensure fair judgement of her act. Thai artists Mang x Daou experienced wardrobe malfunctions during their ballad Aroma, though this didn’t affect their chances in the voting – Thailand came in second place, with 169 points. Why not Asiavision? If Europe has Eurovision, why can’t Asia have Asiavision? For one, the name “Asiavision” is already taken: it’s the broadcasting network of the Asia-Pacific Broadcasting Union (ABU), which has its own song contests and festivals. But mostly, it’s about branding. Although the name Eurovision has become synonymous with the song contest, it actually refers to the European Broadcasting Union’s (EBU) pan-European telecommunications network. The Eurovision Song Contest was created in 1956 to promote the network and attract audiences across borders. (No, it was not created to unite a war-torn Europe.) The purpose of Eurovision Asia is specifically to expand the Eurovision brand and format into the region. This is a project the EBU has been attempting for more than two decades. It plans to continue the expansion of the brand through other continental editions. MANG x DAOU rehearsing for Thailand at Eurovision Song Contest Asia in Bangkok. Ralph Larmann/Eurovision The future of Eurovision Asia Staging the inaugural competition is one thing, but securing the longevity of the franchise in Asia is another matter. Buy-in from economic powerhouses Japan, China and India may be the key to its success. Negotiations were underway with China and Japan to participate this year, and organisers are optimistic that they and several others will join in 2027. The broad geographical scope of “Asia” also has the potential to draw in participants from the Middle East. But broader participation presents its own challenges. The original Eurovision is heavily associated with LGBTQIA+ acceptance and pride, which may not be well-received by certain broadcasters and their audiences within Asia. We saw this play out in the inaugural Eurovision Asia contest: Malaysian broadcaster TV3 cut drag performer Vice Ganda, the Phillipines’ jury spokesperson, from its broadcast. There was also speculation about whether Islamophobia played a role in Malaysia’s Aina Abdul’s results; despite being a favourite to win going into the contest, she finished in fourth place. Soft power and pop Like the OG Eurovision, Eurovision Asia offers great potential for soft power politics. It also has the potential to be a powerful global platform for Asian pop. The inaugural competition was a diverse showcase for the unique voices and cultures of its participants, beyond the dominant trends of J- and K-pop. Hopefully we will get a chance to see more in Manila next year. Jess Carniel does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

d2ec6581b65c222b: International executives will gather in Kuala Lumpur on Nov 16-17 to discuss cruise opportunities in Malaysia and Southeast Asia. For Malaysia, this is a significant development.
It is the first time the event is being hosted here, reflecting the growing recognition of Malaysia's considerable potential to have a more important role in the regional cruise tourism industry.

The event, Seatrade Cruise Asia 2026, brings together more than 18 international cruise line brands, including some of the biggest names such as Royal Caribbean International, StarDream Cruises, Norwegian Cruise Line, MSC Cruises, Azamara, Disney Cruise Line and Princess Cruises.

Senior executives and industry representatives from Europe, the US and Asia will participate in discussions on the future of cruising in this region, including new itineraries, emerging destinations, home-porting opportunities, port infrastructure and the growing demand for cruise holidays among Asian travellers.

Indeed, the event is being organised across several Malaysian destinations, with Kuala Lumpur hosting the main conference, followed by activities in Penang and Langkawi. This provides an opportunity to showcase not just our ports but also the country's wider tourism attractions.
Malaysia's opportunity

For many years, Singapore has established itself as the principal cruise home port in Southeast Asia. Its strategic location, international airport connectivity, modern cruise terminals and well-developed tourism infrastructure have made it a natural starting point for many international cruise operators.
From Singapore, cruise itineraries frequently extend along the Straits of Malacca, with calls at Melaka, Port Klang, Penang and Langkawi before continuing towards Phuket in Thailand.

Another attractive itinerary, depending on the season and weather conditions, covers the eastern side of the peninsula, with destinations such as Tioman, Redang and neighbouring destinations including Koh Samui in Thailand. Further itineraries can extend towards Cambodia and Vietnam, which includes Sihanoukville, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang.

All these routes offer considerable opportunities for Malaysia. We have the geographical advantage of being located along some of the busiest and most established maritime tourism corridors in Southeast Asia.
We also have a diverse range of destinations, from historical cities and cultural attractions to islands, beaches, rainforests and natural landscapes.

However, geographical location alone does not guarantee success. Cruise operators are commercial businesses. They look at passenger demand, port accessibility, terminal facilities, operating costs, immigration procedures, shore excursions and the overall attractiveness of destinations before deciding where to deploy their vessels.
Growing Asian market
The timing is particularly important because the Asian cruise market is developing rapidly.

According to figures released by the Singapore Tourism Board, Southeast Asia recorded approximately 3.9 million cruise passenger visits in 2024. Singapore accounted for 48% of these visits, while Malaysia captured approximately 22%.
Together, the two countries accounted for around 70% of the growing regional market. These figures also demonstrate that Malaysia is already an important cruise destination.

However, it has also been suggested that there is considerable room to grow, particularly if we can attract more international cruise operators and encourage more Malaysians to experience cruise holidays.

The potential domestic market should not be underestimated either. Malaysia has a sizeable middle-income population, an expanding travelling public and a growing number of families looking for alternative holiday experiences.

Cruise holidays could become increasingly attractive, particularly for families who prefer an all-inclusive holiday package with accommodation, meals, entertainment and multiple destinations incorporated into one journey.
There is also an opportunity to develop more regional cruise packages catering specifically to Malaysian, Indonesian, Thai and other Southeast Asian travellers.
This is a growing market that cruise operators are looking to explore and I think Malaysia is ready for it.

a8becbed55c716fd: On Saturday, Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Ismail Lasim confirmed he had withdrawn a letter sent to the Keeper of the Rulers’ Seal concerning the “removal” of Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan.
The letter was also understood to affirm the unanimous support of the 10 sacked executive council members for Tuanku Muhriz.

This brings us to the million-ringgit question: can we trust Negeri Sembilan Umno? Is there any sincerity in what they say? Or is this yet another sleight of hand in an attempt to topple the state ruler?
Tuanku Muhriz's recent public rebuke of Ismail does not paint the latter as someone trustworthy.
There are four reasons why I remain wary of Ismail’s actions.

1. Why is Ismail retracting the letter only now? My theory is that he needs the ruler’s consent to convene the state assembly. While one could, on paper, administer a state without executive councillors, a state assembly sitting is needed to pass budgets and proposed laws.
Which raises this question: is Ismail really remorseful for his actions? Or is he acting out of desperation?
2. Ismail’s actions amid the controversy

They speak volumes about the man himself. He previously said he was coerced into signing a document deposing Tuanku Muhriz, only to later endorse a state executive council statement announcing the ruler’s purported removal.
On Aug 2, Ismail took his oath of office as menteri besar and pledged allegiance to Tuanku Muhriz before signing a proclamation the following day to remove the ruler.
There is a saying, “once bitten, twice shy”. In this instance though, we should be shy four times over.
3. There is still the matter of the other undangs (traditional territorial chieftains), some of whom have been removed, and the matter of the person whom they appointed as the state’s new ruler.

This faction, which is still alive and kicking, has apparently shown no remorse for its actions by openly challenging a Dewan Keadilan dan Undang Negeri Sembilan gazette notice formalising the removal of two chieftains and a customary leader.
It is said that this faction is close to Umno assemblymen in Negeri Sembilan. Mind you, none of the Umno assemblymen have come out to publicly distance themselves from this faction.
So how can we, the people, have any faith in Ismail’s retraction of a letter when Umno is presumably still linked to the said faction?

4. Has Ismail provided assurance via a written and signed declaration that he and his band of Umno men will never again conspire with others to overthrow Tuanku Muhriz? If Ismail were truly repentant, he would have gone the extra mile to show it.

Now, Umno’s decisive win at the Melaka polls will give the party some bragging rights following the controversies over former prime minister Najib Razak’s house arrest and the finances of Felda or Tabung Haji, which did not dent support for the party.
A resurgent Umno is likely to be emboldened to pull off another stunt in Negeri Sembilan, seeing as how the first one didn’t pan out exactly as they planned.
Ismail Lasim and Negeri Sembilan Umno give me very little reason to trust this mea culpa.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
5a2587b6eab93678: Sabtu lalu, Menteri Besar Negeri Sembilan, Ismail Lasim, mengesahkan beliau telah menarik balik surat yang dihantar kepada Penyimpan Mohor Besar Raja-raja berhubung 'penyingkiran' Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan.
Surat itu juga difahamkan mengesahkan sokongan sebulat suara bekas 10 anggota Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri terhadap Tuanku Muhriz.

Ini membawa kita kepada soalan satu juta ringgit: Bolehkah kita meletakkan kepercayaan kepada Umno Negeri Sembilan? Adakah kata-kata mereka benar-benar ikhlas? Atau adakah ini satu lagi helah untuk cuba menjatuhkan pemerintah negeri?
Teguran terbuka Tuanku Muhriz terhadap Ismail baru-baru ini secara tidak langsung menggambarkan Ismail sebagai seorang yang tidak boleh dipercayai.
Terdapat empat sebab mengapa saya masih sangsi terhadap tindakan Ismail.

1. Kenapa baru sekarang Ismail menarik balik surat itu? Teori saya ialah beliau memerlukan perkenan untuk mengadakan sidang DUN. Walaupun dari segi teori menteri besar boleh mentadbir sesebuah negeri tanpa anggota Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri, sidang DUN diperlukan untuk meluluskan belanjawan dan rang undang-undang.
Perkara ini menimbulkan persoalan: adakah Ismail benar-benar insaf atas tindakannya? Atau beliau hanya terdesak?
2. Tindakan Ismail ketika kontroversi itu

Tindakan Ismail menggambarkan dengan jelas mengenai beliau. Sebelum ini, Ismail berkata beliau dipaksa menandatangani dokumen untuk menurunkan Tuanku Muhriz, namun kemudian menyokong kenyataan Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri yang mengumumkan pemerintah negeri itu telah diturunkan.

Pada 2 Ogos, Ismail mengangkat sumpah sebagai menteri besar di hadapan Tuanku Muhriz dan melafazkan ikrar taat setia kepada baginda. Sehari selepas itu, Ismail menandatangani pengisytiharan untuk menurunkan pemerintah negeri itu.
Ada pepatah yang berbunyi, 'sekali terkena, dua kali beringat'. Namun, dalam keadaan ini, kita sepatutnya empat kali beringat.
3. Isu Undang Luak yang masih belum selesai
Masih terdapat isu membabitkan Undang Luak, termasuk beberapa orang yang telah diturunkan, serta individu yang dilantik oleh mereka sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar yang baharu.

Kumpulan ini masih rancak dengan aktiviti mereka, dilihat tidak menunjukkan sebarang kekesalan atas tindakan mereka apabila secara terbuka mencabar notis warta Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU) yang mengesahkan penyingkiran dua Undang dan seorang pemimpin adat.
Dikatakan kumpulan ini mempunyai hubungan rapat dengan Adun Umno Negeri Sembilan. Perlu diingat, tiada seorang pun Adun Umno tampil secara terbuka menolak kumpulan tersebut.
Jadi, bagaimana kita sebagai rakyat boleh menaruh kepercayaan terhadap tindakan Ismail menarik balik surat itu sedangkan Umno dipercayai masih mempunyai kaitan dengan kumpulan berkenaan?

4. Adakah Ismail memberikan jaminan melalui perisytiharan bertulis yang ditandatangani bahawa beliau dan kumpulan anggota Umnonya tidak akan sekali-kali lagi berpakat dengan pihak lain untuk menjatuhkan Tuanku Muhriz? Jika Ismail benar-benar insaf, beliau sepatutnya menunjukkan lebih untuk membuktikannya.

Kini, kemenangan besar Umno dalam PRN Melaka akan memberikan parti itu sedikit kelebihan untuk berbangga susulan kontroversi isu tahanan rumah bekas perdana menteri Najib Razak serta kewangan Felda dan Lembaga Tabung Haji, yang tidak menjejaskan sokongan terhadap parti itu.
Umno yang kembali bangkit berkemungkinan lebih berani untuk melakukan satu lagi tindakan serupa di Negeri Sembilan, memandangkan percubaan pertama mereka tidak berjalan seperti yang dirancang.
Tak banyak sebab untuk saya mempercayai Ismail dan Umno Negeri Sembilan ini benar-benar insaf dengan kesalahan mereka.

13c955d113761972: It began, as most modern Malaysian sagas do, not with a bang, but with a grumble. A mamak shop, that near-sacred 24-hour temple of roti canai and teh tarik, had the audacity to close its doors on Deepavali day.

The reason? To allow its staff, many of whom are Hindus, to celebrate the Festival of Lights. A simple, humane and frankly logical decision. And yet, within hours, it had ignited a firestorm on social media, transforming a shop’s holiday schedule into a national debate on race, religion and the soul of our nation.
This can only happen in Malaysia. “Mamak tutup? On Deepavali? How can a Muslim-run restaurant close for a Hindu-based celebration?” So began the stream of religious insults and slurs.

For most people, the mamak shop is more than a restaurant; it is a cultural institution, a neutral ground where everyone can sit side-by-side at 3am, arguing over football or who should be the prime minister.

But the debate triggered by the post made out the closure to be almost a betrayal of the social contract. The real fireworks began when the keyboard warriors logged on and the debate fractured along predictable, yet deeply depressing, lines.

On one side, some who described the closure as an act of placing Deepavali celebrations over Islam, an analogy that is mind-boggling. On the other side, those who celebrated the closure as a victory for inclusivity, while simultaneously weaponising it against the owners. A simple act of employee appreciation became a truncheon in the never-ending racial culture war.

The comments sections devolved into a cesspool of racial slurs and religious mockery. The practices of each community – from fasting to praying to celebrating – were dissected, mocked and used as ammunition.

This is the Malaysian paradox. We are a nation that prides itself on our diversity, our muhibbah spirit and our ability to live together. We celebrate each other's festivals with open houses and open hearts. But the moment a minor racial or religious issue is raised, the harmony ruptures and the nation's ugly, tribalistic underbelly is exposed for all to see.

The debate exposed a deep-seated insecurity, the fear of being marginalised, anxiety over the “other” and the constant, exhausting need to assert one's own identity in a multi-racial landscape. The mamak shop became a proxy for a much larger, unresolved national conversation about what it means to be Malaysian.

The fact that we lose our minds over such a small matter is precisely the problem. We have become experts at finding offence, at drawing battle lines over the most trivial of issues. A shop closure becomes a religious war. A wrong word becomes a racial slur. A difference in opinion becomes a declaration of enmity.
We are so quick to insult each other, yet so slow to extend the basic courtesy of understanding.

The next time you see a shop closed for a holiday that isn't “yours”, take a breath. Instead of reaching for your phone to type a scathing comment, maybe reach for a packet of murukku from a Hindu neighbour.
The mamak shop will reopen, but the damage done by our own intolerance, the scars we inflict on our national psyche with every hateful comment, are far harder to heal.
Only in Malaysia can a day of light be turned into a war of darkness. Sadly, that is the most Malaysian thing of all.

4e3b3836efc8ff88: From Hisham Aziz

The corporate anxieties following the tabling of Budget 2027 prompt a critical question: when did Malaysia’s apex industry associations transform from champions of free-market resilience into professional victims of helplessness?
The press releases and policy papers issued by the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers (FMM) suffer from structural issues that expose their lack of analytical weight and credibility.

FMM’s press statements exhibit the distinct characteristics of automated text generation — relying heavily on template-driven headers, passive phrasing, and generic buzzword aggregation like “supply chain resilience” and “digital transformation” in place of plant-level operational data. This reliance on high-level abstraction obscures true empirical rigor.

Rather than presenting detailed microeconomic data, unit-cost offsets, or lead-time data, FMM’s advocacy frequently uses sweeping language backed by disproportionately small survey sample sizes to demand massive policy concessions like credit lines, grant facilities, and tax deferments.
To the public and policymakers, organisations like FMM present themselves as fragile, over-burdened entities teetering on the edge of ruin due to basic regulatory adjustments.

Yet, a glance at public policy performance reveals an entirely different reality. These bodies represent the primary beneficiaries of decades of state largesse — enjoying extensive energy subsidies, infrastructure support, and generous tax incentives.

Under Budget 2027, this patronage continues unabated with fresh financing facilities from Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) alongside a transitional exemption from the RM2,000 minimum wage threshold for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
Despite this comprehensive safety net, the lobbying apparatus remains ever unquenchable.

In October 2026, FMM publicly expressed deep disappointment, lamenting a “lack of support” for the manufacturing sector simply because the government did not grant their requested RM1.5 billion extra support package. The danger lies not just in this sense of entitlement, but in the dubious, lightweight methodologies used to justify it.

Consider the statistical acrobatics deployed to influence national economic policy. In June 2026, FMM issued sweeping, alarmist warnings about global supply chain shocks — specifically the impact of the Strait of Hormuz conflict on domestic oil prices and SME survival.
The data to back these massive macroeconomic warnings? A survey pool of exactly 196 companies (FMM Geopolitical Impact Survey, June 2026).
To suggest that a survey pool smaller than a single mid-size factory floor can accurately reflect the structural vulnerabilities of Malaysia’s entire SME sector is absurd.
Yet, it is precisely on the back of these minuscule data sets that case studies are built to demand more credit lines, heavier grants, and broad credit deferments from the taxpayer.

This audacity reaches its peak when looking at their tax advocacy. In their September 2026 Business Conditions Survey (1H2026) briefing, FMM aggressively pushed for a return to the Goods and Services Tax (GST) but demanded it be implemented at a rock-bottom introductory rate of 3.0% — down from the historic 6% floor.
According to FMM’s own polling, while 68% of respondents demanded a rate below 5%, a full 41% explicitly called for a 3% rate.

How peak industrial representatives can genuinely look at Malaysia’s expanding national expenditure and rising infrastructure commitments and suggest halving consumption tax revenues is a great wonder.
They demand that public tax collection be gutted for their operational convenience, while simultaneously expecting the public purse to keep funding their multi-billion-ringgit economic safety nets.
FMM’s platform runs completely counter to the Madani government’s explicit agenda to transition Malaysia away from its unhealthy dependency on low-cost, low-skilled migrant labour.
By fighting tooth and nail against statutory wage floors and basic family protections, FMM is actively working to keep Malaysian wages artificially suppressed.
This short-sighted resistance eliminates the exact economic pressure businesses need to innovate.

If labour is kept artificially cheap through state exemptions and structural suppression, manufacturing firms will feel zero urgency to invest in research and development (R&D), upgrade their technology, or pursue genuine, automation-led productivity growth.
It is not possible to build an Industry 4.0 economy on an automated AI-generated script that begs to preserve an Industry 2.0 labour pool.
This irony peaks when looking at how FMM constructs its internal narratives.
In that same 1H2026 Survey, FMM dedicated an entire section to aggressively policing government administration, using curated survey questions to put HRD Corp in a distinctly negative light.

FMM explicitly complained that HRD Corp’s revised e-TRiS grant conditions actively “hindered training and planning” for 44% of businesses, highlighting that rigid bureaucratic rules — like the mandatory 14-day advance approval window — made it nearly impossible to provide urgent training.

FMM will meticulously poll its members to complain about public sector administrative flexibility, and they will rightfully demand accountability following HRD Corp’s financial mismanagement scandals.

Yet, they weaponize these administrative hurdles as a convenient shield to demand that training funds remain entirely under corporate autonomy. We see this exact transactional morality in their response to parental benefits.

While FMM aggressively fought the statutory 98-day maternity leave mandate as an unbearable operational cost when forced to pay for it, they happily celebrate the newly proposed Budget 2027 post-maternity allowance simply because the state is funding it through the Employment Insurance System (EIS).

They expect national tax revenues to be minimised and public funding maximised whenever it protects their corporate ledger but completely reject socioeconomic flexibility when asked to internally finance a liveable wage or grant a recovering mother an extra month of leave.
The government must stop treating these large corporate blocks as fragile patients in need of permanent economic life support.
True economic restructuring requires rigorous data, authentic feedback, and shared sacrifice. Not fake narratives and political manipulation.
Policymakers should look past the AI-generated statements and reports based on questionable methodologies and unreliable sample sizes and look closely at the empirical reality.

Malaysia’s industrial sector is well-capitalised and heavily subsidised. It is time they scaled up through innovation, automation, and R&D, rather than lobbying their way out of basic social contracts.
Malaysia’s manufacturing cannot be on permanent life-support to pander to a small group of people, nor held ransom by people using trade associations for their political agenda.
Hisham Aziz is an FMT reader.

8a6b39297448afa6: From Sadiq Asyraf

When Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi left the hall at the Melaka International Trade Centre on Saturday night, he was not sent off with a victory song. Barisan Nasional supporters chanted one word, over and over: "Bubar!" Dissolve.

Umno still sits in the unity coalition government, and its president is one of the two deputy prime ministers. But since September, BN has said it will leave the government the moment Parliament is dissolved.

Spontaneous or not, the chant fits Umno's position all year, which might be called minimum loyalty: do exactly what the coalition agreement requires and nothing more. That lets Umno push the government towards the edge without pulling it down itself.
Minimum loyalty

Umno information chief Azalina Othman Said set out the limits the day before polling. On her reading, the agreement obliges Umno to back the prime minister only on confidence votes, supply bills and procedural motions touching the government's legitimacy. Beyond that, Umno is free to disagree.

That reading covers Umno's conduct this year: going solo in Johor, partnering Perikatan Nasional in Negeri Sembilan and Melaka, and defending the conditional pardon of former prime minister Najib Razak against DAP's objections. All of it sits within the letter of the agreement.
Umno supplies just enough votes to keep the government standing while campaigning against its partners in the states. The unity government now rests more on seat arithmetic than on trust.

Azalina answered DAP's call for Umno ministers to resign with four options: mediate, stay calm, end the agreement, or review the clause on Islam, the Malays and the Rulers at the risk of unpredictable consequences.

With no termination clause in the agreement, Azalina presented dissolution as the logical political outcome. But ending a coalition agreement does not, by itself, constitutionally require Parliament to be dissolved. The next move, she told DAP, was theirs.
Read together, the options allow Umno to shift to Pakatan Harapan much of the immediate political cost of a rupture.

On Tuesday, Zahid said he would rather see Parliament dissolved than the Cabinet reshuffled. On Thursday, after DAP's challenge, he said BN still backed Anwar Ibrahim federally. On Saturday, his victory press conference spoke of a hattrick and, according to media reports, not of dissolution. About 40 minutes later, his supporters at the MITC entrance said it for him.

Unless the leadership distances itself from the chant, it is one message sent through two channels. Agenda-setting theory explains why the second channel matters: the media may not decide what audiences think, but they shape what audiences think about. Supporters filmed and shared the "Bubar!" clips themselves.

The likely effect is to shift attention from BN's victory in a state contest to the stability of the federal government. The question of the week becomes when Parliament will be dissolved, and it is the prime minister, rather than Umno, who is pressed to answer it.

PH plays the same game. Two nights before polling, Anwar quipped that some government critics sat beside him in Cabinet, then said he was not targeting Zahid. The same night, defending DAP, he asked whether it was DAP that had been responsible for the problems at Tabung Haji, Felda and 1MDB, a pointed reference to administrations led by his own federal partner.
After the results, he offered congratulations and cooperation. Both partners campaign against each other, then make up on paper.
The dissolution trap

Melaka gave the dissolution push its evidence. According to official results, BN won 21 seats, PN three and PH four, all of them urban DAP seats. BN matched its 2021 tally, and the combined BN and PN vote share barely moved, at about 63%.

The difference is that BN and PN no longer split their votes by contesting against one another. PH's share fell from 35.7 to 29.3%. Its candidates in Ayer Limau and Serkam lost their deposits with less than 12% of the vote.
That shifts bargaining power: PH has struggled to demonstrate electoral strength in Malay-majority constituencies, while Umno remains the government's principal Malay political partner.

The strategy has limits. PN won three of its five allotted seats, including Bukit Katil from PH. Outside government, Umno would face the same PN partners for Malay-majority seats at GE16 without the advantages of office.

Minimum loyalty pays best while Umno is inside the government. That creates a strong incentive for Umno to let PH initiate any rupture, so that it can present itself as the party that honoured the agreement until the end.

For Anwar, every exit has a price. Dissolving now means facing BN and PN together at PH's weakest point, after setbacks in Sabah, Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka. Holding on lets Umno enjoy power in Putrajaya while building the story of a government clinging to office.

Some DAP supporters want Umno ministers sacked. Whether the government could survive without BN's MPs depends on parliamentary arithmetic that has shifted this year. But the case for keeping Umno is political as much as numerical: it is the government's principal Malay political partner. Melaka suggests that value is under strain, and sacking Umno would simply set it free.
Whatever Anwar decides, minimum loyalty gives Umno a ready story. Sacked, it leaves as the betrayed partner. If Parliament is dissolved, it is merely keeping its promise to the king.

The unity government may yet be reshaped or run its full term. But if the partnership does break, the contest that matters will be over who controls the story of the separation. On Saturday night, Umno's supporters showed they intend to write the first draft.
Sadiq Asyraf is a political communication and media warfare analyst.

5c717fc19e0cf4c7: People are taking to the streets across the world. In 2025, mass mobilisation occurred in countries such as Morocco, Tanzania and Turkey. In Madagascar, protests resulted in president Andry Rajoelina fleeing the country in October. More recently, protesters have filled the streets from France and Italy to Senegal and Kenya. By mass mobilisation, we mean sustained, organised campaigns of protests that involve more than 1,000 people, aimed at changing a country’s political regime or removing the government or leader. Mass mobilisation has historically been seen as a viable path to democracy. Ferdinand Marcos left Manila in 1986 after weeks of popular protests. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 after months of demonstrations in East Germany. South Africa’s apartheid regime yielded to domestic and international pressure in the 1990s. The examples are many, and mass movements have been a driving force to democratic change in authoritarian regimes. Yet the historical record is less clear-cut. We are researchers who study protest and democratisation. In a recent study, together with colleagues Kristian Skrede Gleditsch (University of Essex) and Gudmund Hermansen (University of Oslo), we examine how mass mobilisation influenced the likelihood of democratic transitions between 1900 and 2019. We find that the well-documented relationship between mass mobilisation and democratisation largely belongs to a historical golden age, stretching from the early 1980s until roughly the Arab Spring in 2011. During this period, mass mobilisation was strongly associated with both democratisation and regime change. Before and after this golden age, however, we find no detectable relationship between mass mobilisation and democratic change. The two periods are nevertheless not identical. Before 1980, mass mobilisation made rulers more likely to fall. But the regimes that fell were not systematically replaced by democracies. In other words, mobilisation could topple a regime, but not necessarily bring about democratic change. One example is Ethiopia’s 1974 revolution. Mass protests and strikes contributed to the overthrow of Haile Selassie, only for the monarchy to be replaced by a military dictatorship rather than democracy. Today, the pattern is different. From the Arab Spring through 2019, mass mobilisation is no longer systematically associated with regime collapse. Authoritarian regimes have managed to remain in power despite extensive mobilisation. Major waves of protest have challenged incumbent regimes without bringing them down. Authoritarian leaders increasingly appear capable of riding out even large-scale popular mobilisation. Examples include Belarus, Iran and Togo, At the same time, we are witnessing exceptionally high levels of popular mobilisation. The fact that it no longer has the same democratising effect helps explain how a wave of protest can coincide with the current authoritarian wave. Understanding why mass mobilisation on democratisation has become less effective is one of the most important questions for understanding the development of democracy in our time. Why has mass mobilisation become less effective? The short answer is that we do not know for certain. To examine how the effectiveness of mass mobilisation has changed over time, we combined data on protest campaigns demanding democratic change to classify countries as democracies or autocracies in each year. We focused only on autocracies, examining whether mass mobilisation increased the likelihood of a transition to democracy. Unlike previous studies, we used statistical models that allowed the effect of mass mobilisation to vary over time, rather than assuming it remained constant. We also tested whether our findings depended on a few influential cases. More than 20 campaigns that were followed by democratic transitions during the golden age would have had to end without democratisation to substantially flatten the peak. Similarly, around 10 unsuccessful campaigns after 2010 would have needed to result in democratic transitions to substantially reduce the observed decline. The overall pattern also held when we excluded individual regions from the analysis. We find little support for several suggested explanations. Trends in campaign size, the diversity of participants, coordinated leadership, state repression, and where protests take place do not coincide with the rise and fall in protest effectiveness. However, our measures are relatively crude, so we cannot rule out that these factors played a role. But they are unlikely to explain the broader pattern on their own. What we can show is that the power of mass mobilisation to bring about democratic change has shifted dramatically over time. What we cannot say with certainty is why its golden age began, or why it came to an end. Some scholars have suggested that today’s movements may have become overly dependent on social media and large demonstrations, whereas effective resistance requires deeper organisation, a wider range of tactics, and long-term relationship-building. Our data do not capture these factors well enough to provide a decisive test of that argument. At the same time, authoritarian regimes may have become better at responding to challenges from the street. New information technologies make it easier to monitor opposition movements and identify key individuals. This facilitates what researchers call smart repression: more targeted and subtle forms of coercion. The international climate may also have contributed to this shift. The golden age coincided with the end of the cold war and stronger international pressure for democratic reform. But since the Arab Spring, western countries have increasingly chosen stability and security cooperation over democratic reform. At the same time, authoritarian regimes have gained access to alternative sources of support. Contemporary autocracies operate through international networks that provide one another with money, technology, propaganda and diplomatic backing. They may strengthen regimes’ capacity to withstand mass mobilisation. Read more: When bad rulers go, do their families face justice and is there reform? Six African case studies Our study doesn’t conclusively test these explanations. Together, however, they suggest that the rise and fall in the effectiveness of mass mobilisation is unlikely to be explained by any single factor. Perhaps the pendulum has begun to swing back? Nor can we say with certainty what effect mass mobilisation has on democratisation today. Our analysis ends in 2019. We do not know whether the weak relationship we observe at the end of the period has persisted, or whether the pendulum has started to swing back. Historically, the impact of mass mobilisation has moved in cycles. It was by no means obvious in the 1970s that the world was on the verge of a golden age of democratic mobilisation. Since 2019, moreover, we have seen several important victories for mass mobilisation. In Bangladesh, Sheikh Hasina was forced from power following extensive student protests. In Serbia, nearly two years of student-led protests culminated in an electoral victory that ended Aleksandar Vučić’s long hold on power. In South Korea, popular mobilisation helped stop President Yoon Suk Yeol’s attempt to sideline democracy. And in Poland and Hungary, broad democratic mobilisation has formed part of a wider resistance to governments that ultimately lost power through elections. Read more: Senegal’s ruling alliance has split: will political turmoil follow? In Senegal, mass protests in 2024 helped thwart President Macky Sall’s attempt to remain in power beyond his constitutional mandate. In Malawi, mass protests against electoral irregularities, alongside judicial intervention, paved the way for an opposition victory in the 2020 rerun election. Democratic courage is therefore clearly not in short supply. Researchers may try to understand what is required, but it is above all those who continue to organise, demonstrate and demand democratic rights and freedom for everyone who can ensure that it happens. Ida Rudolfsen receives funding from the Research Council of Norway. Marianne Dahl receives funding from Research Council of Norway
39994499436d36ce: Drawing upon Lord Denning’s advocacy of common sense in judicial decisions – alongside my own worldly and judicial experience in Malaysia, rooted in my origins in Thopputhurai, Vedaranyam, Tamil Nadu, India – I will state bluntly: no person operating in isolation possesses the capacity to defraud a nation on a scale that attracts universal infamy without the active assistance of a wider network.

When I sat as a judge, I treated common sense as my primary guiding principle when interpreting the Federal Constitution, the law and the facts of any case. It was strictly through this practical approach that I developed the oath of office jurisprudence as well as the concept of university-cum-court annexed arbitration.

With his 38-year career on the English bench, Denning earned the title of “the people’s judge”. At the heart of his jurisprudence was a simple, powerful conviction: the law is neither an abstract puzzle for academics nor a rigid trap for ordinary citizens.
Instead, he advocated, judges and lawyers must apply practical common sense to achieve real justice when interpreting both statutes and facts.
Among his many judgments grounded in common sense, I was particularly guided by his approach in Butler Machine Tool Co Ltd v Ex-Cell-O Corp (England) Ltd.

In resolving commercial contract disputes, Denning advocated looking at the entirety of the documents to determine what a sensible businessperson would understand, rather than applying rigid, artificial formulas.

Regarding the SRC International case, I have previously written that, among other critical issues, Najib Razak was deprived of procedural fairness and his constitutional right to counsel. Common sense dictates that procedural fairness is a core pillar of the criminal justice system and our constitutional framework.

Furthermore, it is a fallacy for certain commentators to circulate articles suggesting that a single Malay individual could orchestrate a massive fraud against the nation entirely on his own without the involvement of non-Malay enablers and professionals.

In my view, it is a travesty of justice to paint a picture suggesting that one person possessed the solitary capability to execute a grand-scale national scam without the active participation of accomplices across different communities.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
